about: Afuera model syllabus for Mexican Spanish, A1–C1 (docs/teach-plan.md → Magda). Built 2026-10-22 from every source read in full (ELE Actual A1; Nuevo Español en Marcha Básico A1–A2; Seven Keys: Communicating in Mexico; Mexican Spanish Word Power; the Plan Curricular del Instituto Cervantes A1–C2, adapted from Spain's Spanish to Mexico's), lined up and reordered for a newcomer living in Mexico, then reviewed by a second teacher. About the language and real-life situations only, not the game's places or mechanics. Readable version: docs/syllabus-es-mx.md. Word list: content/es-mx/syllabus-words.csv.

units.title: Greet and take leave
units.can_do: Greet people and say goodbye at any time of day, with usted by default and tú with people your age who use it first.
functions: greet everyone when you walk into a room
situations: walking into a shop or a waiting room and greeting everyone
meeting a neighbour by the door
greeting an older person or an official

frames.es: ¡Buenos días!
frames.en: Good morning!
frames.note: Until about noon. Buen día is also common.

frames.es: ¡Buenas tardes! / ¡Buenas noches!
frames.en: Good afternoon! / Good evening!
frames.note: Buenas tardes from about noon until dark; buenas noches once it's dark, as hello and as goodbye.

frames.es: Buenas.
frames.en: Hi.
frames.note: Short and safe at any time of day: walking into a shop, a waiting room or a lift.

frames.es: Buenos días, señora. ¿Cómo está?
frames.en: Good morning, ma'am. How are you?
frames.note: Usted: strangers, older people, shopkeepers, officials.

frames.es: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?
frames.en: Very well, thanks. And you?

frames.es: ¿Qué tal? / ¿Cómo estás?
frames.en: How's it going? / How are you?
frames.note: Tú: friends, children, and people your age who use tú with you first.

frames.es: Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?
frames.en: Fine, thanks. And you?

frames.es: Hasta luego. Que le vaya bien.
frames.en: Bye. Have a good day.
frames.note: Lit. may it go well for you. With tú: Que te vaya bien.

frames.es: Gracias, igualmente.
frames.en: Thanks, same to you.
frames.note: The reply to que le vaya bien.

frames.es: ¡Nos vemos! / ¡Hasta mañana!
frames.en: See you! / See you tomorrow!

grammar.point: usted and tú as two sets of chunks
grammar.explain: Mexican Spanish has a polite 'you' (usted), the default with adults you don't know, and a friendly 'you' (tú); usted takes the same verb form as 'he' or 'she'.

examples.es: Que le vaya bien. / Que te vaya bien.

grammar.trap: In Mexico usted is respect, not stiffness: tú with an older stranger, a shopkeeper or an official sounds overfamiliar. Wait until the other person uses tú with you.

grammar.explain: To say how you are, Spanish uses estar, not ser.

examples.en: I'm a bit tired. (a woman speaking)

grammar.trap: English 'I am fine' tempts you to say 'soy bien', which is wrong. Say 'estoy bien'.

grammar.explain: Buenos días until about noon, buenas tardes until dark, and buenas noches after dark, both as hello and as goodbye; buenas is a short form for any time.

examples.es: ¡Buenas noches! (8 p.m., walking into a shop)
examples.en: Good evening! (8 p.m., walking into a shop)

grammar.trap: Buenas noches isn't only for bedtime: it's the normal hello after dark. And buenas tardes starts at noon, earlier than English 'good afternoon' feels.

grammar.explain: To talk to two or more people, Mexicans always use ustedes, with the 'they' form of the verb, even with friends and children.

examples.en: Have a good day. (to a group)

grammar.trap: Vosotros (¿cómo estáis?) is Spain only; in Mexico it sounds foreign. Use ustedes and están.

grammar.point: que le vaya bien as a fixed goodbye
grammar.explain: Learn it whole: change only le, te or les for the person; the verb form is explained much later.
grammar.trap: Don't rebuild it from English 'have a nice day'; the whole phrase is the Mexican goodbye, and the answer is 'gracias, igualmente'.

vocabulary.en: good evening, good night (after dark; hello and goodbye)
to be (how you are, where you are)
young woman, miss; also to a waitress or shop assistant
respectful title before an older person's first name (don Pepe, doña Carmen)

pronunciation: Spanish has five short, pure vowels that never glide: bue-nos dí-as, not 'bway-nohz dee-ahs'. Say e and o without the English 'ey' and 'oh-oo' glide: bien, noches, cómo.
Mexicans keep a clear, strong s, and z or c before e and i also sound like s: gracias is 'grah-syahs', and the final s of buenas noches is fully pronounced.

common_errors.why: How you are takes estar, not ser.
Strangers and older people get usted, with the 'he/she' form of the verb.

common_errors.wrong: ¡Buenas noches! (walking into a shop at 4 p.m.)
common_errors.why: Buenas noches starts when it's dark.
Vosotros isn't used in Mexico; any group gets ustedes.
No article when you speak to someone directly.

units.culture: Mexicans greet when they walk into a small shop, a waiting room or a lift, and say goodbye when they leave; a quick 'buenas' is enough, and silence comes across as cold. When you meet someone, men usually shake hands; in social settings a man and a woman, or two women, usually greet with one light kiss on the right cheek, often from the first meeting, while at work and in offices a handshake is the safe choice. Using usted is a sign of respect, not distance.
units.evidence: Without being prompted, the learner greets on arrival with the right greeting for the time of day, answers ¿cómo está? with (muy) bien, gracias and returns the question in the same register (usted with an older or unfamiliar character, tú with a peer who uses tú first), and leaves with que le vaya bien or nos vemos.
sources: ELE L1 (greetings by time of day), L4 (tú/usted, Mexican usted note, no article when addressing)
EeM U1 (tú/usted, formal and informal greetings)
7K ch.1 (usted as respect, not stiffness), ch.6 (handshake; one kiss on the right cheek)
PCIC Func. A1 5.1, 5.2, 5.21 (greet, reply, take leave); Tác. A1 3.1.1 ([Hispanoamérica] usted, ustedes only); Saberes 1.3, 2.1.5 (greetings by time of day; greeting the room), rewritten for Mexico

units.title: When you don't understand
units.can_do: Say you didn't understand, ask for a repeat, a slower pace, a spelling or a word, and say how much Spanish you speak.
functions: ask someone to write it down
say how much Spanish you speak
situations: someone speaks fast at a counter
spelling your name for a form or an order
an unknown word on a sign
a neighbour uses a word you don't know

frames.es: ¿Mande?
frames.en: Sorry? / Pardon?
frames.note: The polite Mexican way to ask someone to say it again; also how you answer when someone calls your name.

frames.es: Perdón, no entendí.
frames.en: Sorry, I didn't understand.
frames.note: No entiendo (I don't understand) works too.

frames.es: ¿Me lo puede repetir, por favor?
frames.en: Could you say that again, please?
frames.note: With tú: ¿Me lo puedes repetir?

frames.es: Más despacio, por favor.
frames.en: More slowly, please.

frames.es: ¿Qué significa «banqueta»?
frames.en: What does 'banqueta' mean?

frames.es: ¿Cómo se dice «receipt» en español?
frames.en: How do you say 'receipt' in Spanish?

frames.es: ¿Me lo puede escribir?
frames.en: Could you write it down for me?

frames.es: Hablo un poquito de español. Estoy aprendiendo.
frames.en: I speak a little Spanish. I'm learning.

frames.es: ¿Cómo se escribe? ¿Con be grande o con ve chica?
frames.en: How do you spell it? With a B or a V?
frames.note: B and V sound the same, so Mexicans say be grande and ve chica (also be larga, ve corta) to tell them apart.

frames.es: ¿Me deletrea su apellido, por favor?
frames.en: Could you spell your surname, please?

grammar.explain: No entendí, ¿me lo puede repetir? and más despacio work as fixed phrases from day one; no entendí is a past form you'll learn properly in a1-15.
grammar.trap: Don't wait until you understand the grammar: say the chunk exactly as it is, and say it in Spanish rather than switching to English.

grammar.explain: In Mexico ¿mande? is the polite way to ask for a repeat, and also the answer when someone calls your name.
grammar.trap: A bare ¿qué? sounds blunt in Mexico, especially to older people; use ¿mande? or ¿perdón?.

grammar.explain: Lo stands for 'it' and goes before the verb, right after me: me lo repite = repeat it for me.

examples.en: Could you repeat it for me?
Could you write it for me?

grammar.trap: English word order tempts you to put 'it' at the end; keep me lo together before the verb.

grammar.explain: ¿Me puede …? (usted) or ¿Me puedes …? (tú) + a verb in its basic -r form asks someone to do something.
grammar.trap: The second verb stays in the -r form: ¿puede repetir?, not ¿puede repite?.

grammar.point: Spelling aloud with Mexican letter names
grammar.explain: Letters have Spanish names, and Mexicans use special labels for B, V and W when they spell.
grammar.trap: The vowel names are not the English ones: e is 'eh', i is 'ee'. Spell 'Webb' as doble u, e, be grande, be grande.

vocabulary.en: to spell out letter by letter

pronunciation: Keep every vowel short and clear, even unstressed ones: re-pe-tir, des-pa-cio, sig-ni-fi-ca. English speakers tend to swallow them ('r'p'teer'), which makes words hard to recognise.
Seseo: z, and c before e or i, sound like s in Mexico: despacio, dice, gracias. Don't use the 'th' sound of Spain.

common_errors.why: A bare ¿qué? sounds abrupt in Mexico.
Se dice = 'is said'; ¿cómo dice? asks how he or she says it.
After poder the verb stays in the -r form.
Before a noun, un poquito needs de; on its own it's fine: hablo poquito.

common_errors.right: doble u, e, be grande, be grande
common_errors.why: Spanish letter names, with the Mexican labels for W and B.

units.culture: Asking a Mexican '¿me entendiste?' can feel like a test of their intelligence, so people rephrase rather than check. The other side of this is that you, as a newcomer, are expected to ask: ¿mande?, ¿me lo repite? and ¿qué significa…? are normal and well received, and most people slow down and rephrase gladly. Mexicans are generous with foreigners who try to speak Spanish.
recycles: a1-01: usted and tú (¿me lo puede / puedes repetir?)
units.evidence: When the learner misses something, they ask for repair in Spanish (¿mande?, no entendí, ¿me lo puede repetir?, más despacio) instead of switching to English or going silent; they ask what a word means or how to say one, and can spell their name with Spanish letter names.
sources: ELE L1 (Ayudas: no entiendo, ¿cómo se escribe?, spelling dialogue), L2 (¿cómo se dice…?, más despacio)
EeM Antes de empezar (repair kit; ¿con be o con uve?; spelling a surname), U1 transcripts (spelling at reception)
7K ch.1 and ch.4 (¿mande?; don't ask '¿me entendiste?'; the foreigner may ask openly)
PCIC Func. A1 4.1 (más despacio, ¿puedes repetir?); Proc. 1.2.6 (compensation chunks); Ort. A1 (letter names, [México] doble u); Pron. A1–A2 (pure vowels, seseo)

units.title: Introduce yourself as a newcomer
units.can_do: Say your name, where you're from, where you live now and how long you've been here, and swap numbers.
functions: say how long you've been here
situations: meeting a neighbour for the first time

frames.es: Me llamo … ¿Y usted?
frames.en: My name is … And you?
frames.note: With tú: ¿Y tú?

frames.es: ¿Cómo se llama? / ¿Cómo te llamas?
frames.en: What's your name? (usted / tú)

frames.es: Mucho gusto. — Igualmente.
frames.en: Nice to meet you. — Likewise.
frames.note: Encantado (a man) or encantada (a woman) also works.

frames.es: Soy de …, pero ahora vivo aquí.
frames.en: I'm from …, but I live here now.

frames.es: ¿De dónde es usted? / ¿De dónde eres?
frames.en: Where are you from? (usted / tú)

frames.es: Vivo en la colonia …
frames.en: I live in the … neighbourhood.
frames.note: Colonia is the everyday word for a neighbourhood, and part of every address.

frames.es: Llevo dos semanas en México. / Tengo dos semanas aquí.
frames.en: I've been in Mexico for two weeks. / I've been here two weeks.
frames.note: Both are present tense in Spanish; tengo … aquí is the everyday Mexican form.

frames.es: ¿Cuánto tiempo lleva aquí?
frames.en: How long have you been here?
frames.note: With tú: ¿Cuánto tiempo llevas aquí?

frames.es: ¿Tienes WhatsApp? ¿Me pasas tu número?
frames.en: Are you on WhatsApp? Can I have your number?
frames.note: With usted: ¿Tiene WhatsApp? ¿Me pasa su número?

grammar.explain: Me llamo, te llamas and se llama are how Spanish gives names: literally 'I call myself'.
grammar.trap: Don't drop the me: 'llamo Ana' means 'I'm calling Ana'. Mi nombre es … is correct but sounds formal; soy Ana is fine too.

grammar.point: ser de for where you're from
grammar.explain: Soy de + place gives your origin and avoids nationality words, which change for men and women.
grammar.trap: Use ser, not estar: 'estoy de Canadá' is wrong. The question keeps de at the front: ¿de dónde eres?, never '¿dónde eres de?'.

grammar.point: vivir en: present tense for yo, tú, usted
grammar.explain: Regular -ir verbs end in -o for 'I', -es for tú and -e for usted.
grammar.trap: For your home use vivir: vivo en esta colonia. 'Estoy en esta colonia' means you're there right now.

grammar.point: llevar / tener + time for how long
grammar.explain: To say how long you've been somewhere, Spanish uses the present: llevo or tengo + time (+ aquí, en México).

examples.en: I've been in Mexico for three months.
How long have you been here?

grammar.trap: English 'I have been' tempts 'he estado aquí por dos semanas'; Mexicans say llevo dos semanas or tengo dos semanas aquí.

grammar.explain: Question words carry a written accent and come first in the question.

examples.en: How long have you been here?

grammar.trap: Spanish uses ¿cómo? (how), not ¿qué? (what), to ask someone's name: ¿qué te llamas? is wrong.

vocabulary.form: me llamo, se llama, te llamas

vocabulary.en: to be (who you are, where you're from)
with a time: to have been (somewhere)
pleased to meet you (encantada for a woman)
neighbourhood (an official part of every address)

pronunciation: ll and y sound the same in Mexico, like the y in English 'yes': me llamo, llevo, calle.
Yes/no questions rise at the end (¿Tienes WhatsApp?↑) because word order doesn't change; questions with a question word fall (¿De dónde eres?↓).

common_errors.why: Llamarse needs me: 'llamo' alone means 'I call'.
Origin takes ser.

common_errors.wrong: He estado aquí por dos semanas.
common_errors.right: Llevo dos semanas aquí. / Tengo dos semanas aquí.
common_errors.why: Spanish uses the present with llevar or tener for time up to now.
The preposition goes before the question word.
Names are asked with cómo.

units.culture: Mexicans usually ask early on how long you've been here and whether you like it, and are often delighted that you're learning Spanish. Numbers are swapped for WhatsApp, which almost everyone uses, from neighbours to plumbers. Every address includes the colonia (and a postcode, código postal), which matters more than the street name for finding a place.
recycles: a1-02: ¿Cómo se escribe? and spelling aloud
units.evidence: Meeting a character for the first time, the learner gives their name with me llamo, says where they're from with soy de and that they live here now, says how long they've been here with llevo / tengo + time, asks the same back in the right register, and answers mucho gusto with igualmente.
sources: ELE L1–L4 (name, origin, address, phone, introductions; Mexican colonia and celular notes)
EeM U1 ('Sí, pero ahora vivo en…'; gym sign-up), U18 (¿cuánto tiempo llevas…?; dropping the gerund)
7K ch.1 (Mexicans' tolerance of foreigners' Spanish), ch.6 (introductions)
PCIC Func. A1 1.1–1.3 (identify, ask and give information); NE A1 3.1 (identity: colonia, código postal, celular); NG A2 4.2 (desde hace; tengo dos meses aquí [México])

units.title: Everyday courtesy
units.can_do: Use the small words Mexicans expect: ask to pass, excuse yourself, thank and answer thanks, wish people a good meal, address people politely.
situations: squeezing past people on a bus or in a queue
leaving a table where others are still eating

frames.es: Con permiso.
frames.en: Excuse me.
frames.note: Getting past someone, leaving a table or a room, going in ahead of someone. People answer 'Pase' or 'Propio'.

frames.es: Disculpe, ¿me ayuda con algo?
frames.en: Excuse me, could you help me with something?
frames.note: With tú: Disculpa, ¿me ayudas?

frames.es: Perdón. — No pasa nada.
frames.en: Sorry. — It's fine.

frames.es: ¡Provecho!
frames.en: Enjoy your meal!
frames.note: To people eating, as you walk past their table or leave.

frames.es: Gracias. — De nada. / Con mucho gusto.
frames.en: Thanks. — You're welcome. / My pleasure.

frames.es: A sus órdenes.
frames.en: At your service.
frames.note: A polite reply to thanks, or an offer of help, from shop staff and officials.

frames.es: ¡Pásele, joven! ¿Qué buscaba?
frames.en: Come in! What were you looking for?
frames.note: Joven to a younger man; señorita, or güera, to a woman. Pásele = come in, go ahead.

frames.es: Nada más estoy viendo, gracias.
frames.en: I'm just looking, thanks.

frames.es: Un momentito, por favor.

grammar.explain: Con permiso, provecho, disculpe and a sus órdenes are fixed phrases; learn each with the moment it belongs to.

examples.en: Excuse me. (to get past or leave)
Excuse me, could you help me? (to get attention)

grammar.trap: English 'excuse me' covers three Spanish phrases: con permiso to get past or leave, disculpe to get attention, perdón after a bump or a mistake.

grammar.explain: Disculpe goes with usted and disculpa with tú, the same split as ¿cómo está? and ¿cómo estás?.

examples.en: Excuse me, can you help me? (tú)

grammar.trap: With a shopkeeper or a stranger, use disculpe; disculpa is for friends and people your age who use tú.

grammar.explain: Adding -ito or -ita makes a request or an amount sound smaller and politer.

examples.en: Right now / in a little while.

grammar.trap: It doesn't mean literally small: un momentito can be several minutes, and ahorita can mean now, soon or later.

grammar.explain: Mexicans often address people by a title or role instead of a name: joven, señorita, señor, señora, don or doña + first name.

examples.en: Excuse me (to a young man), could you help me?

grammar.trap: Don and doña go with the first name, never the surname, and only for people older than you. Vendors may call you güero or güera; it's friendly sales talk, not a comment on your looks.

grammar.explain: Shop staff ask ¿qué buscaba? or ¿qué necesitaba? in a past form to sound softer; just answer in the present.

examples.en: What were you looking for? — Some batteries.
What can I do for you?

grammar.trap: It doesn't mean they think you've stopped looking; it's simply polite.

vocabulary.en: excuse me (to get past, leave a table or a room)
excuse me (to get attention; usted); disculpa (tú)
young person; how you call a waiter or young shop assistant
fair-haired or light-skinned person; vendors' friendly way to address customers (güera for a woman)

pronunciation: Stress the right syllable: con per-MI-so, pro-VE-cho, dis-CUL-pe, per-DÓN. The written accent on perdón marks a stress the normal rule wouldn't give.
Keep courtesy phrases warm and level. Mexican politeness lives in a soft, even tone; a sharp, high-pitched '¡gracias!' in the English style can sound annoyed.

common_errors.wrong: Disculpe (pushing past people on a bus)
common_errors.why: Con permiso is for getting past or leaving; disculpe is for getting attention.
Don and doña go with the first name.
Strangers get usted.
A translation of 'enjoy your meal' sounds like a waiter; to anyone eating, Mexicans just say provecho.
English 'please' isn't the answer to thanks; use de nada or con mucho gusto.

units.culture: Mexican courtesy is constant and small: con permiso when you pass someone or leave a table, provecho to anyone eating as you walk by (even strangers in a restaurant), and a greeting for the whole room. Shop and market staff call out ¡pásele! and address you as joven, señorita or güero/güera; staff and officials answer thanks with a sus órdenes or con mucho gusto. Getting these small words right earns more goodwill than perfect grammar.
recycles: a1-01: Buenas tardes / Hasta luego / Que le vaya bien
units.evidence: The learner uses con permiso to pass or leave, provecho to people eating, disculpe to get a stranger's attention and perdón after a slip, thanks people and answers thanks with de nada or con mucho gusto, and addresses people with señor, señora, joven or don/doña + first name.
sources: 7K ch.1, ch.4 and §6 (con permiso, provecho, diminutive softeners, muy amable; these items are missing from the other books)
PCIC Func. A1–A2 5.10–5.13 (apologise, thank, reply to thanks), with Mexican swaps (de nada → con mucho gusto, a la orden)
PCIC Func. C1–C2 (a sus órdenes, para servirle; moved down for Mexico, D3)
PCIC Saberes 1.4.2, 2.1.5 (strangers: greet the room, provecho, con permiso), rewritten for Mexico

grammar.explain: Me da + what you want, in the present tense, is the normal polite way to order or buy.

examples.es: Me da un café, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have a coffee, please?
Can I have two steak tacos?

examples.es: Me da una torta para llevar.
examples.en: Can I have a torta to go?

grammar.trap: Quiero … on its own can sound blunt; me da … with por favor is the safe default.

grammar.explain: Nouns are masculine or feminine; plurals add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant.
grammar.trap: Agua is feminine but takes un and el, because it starts with a stressed a: un agua de jamaica, el agua. Adjectives stay feminine: el agua está fría.

grammar.explain: Spanish says what something is filled with or made of using de after the noun.
grammar.trap: Don't put the filling first as in English: 'pastor tacos' becomes tacos de pastor.

grammar.explain: Con (with) and sin (without) go straight before the food, with no article.
grammar.trap: Say sin cebolla, not 'sin la cebolla'.

grammar.explain: In central Mexico ¿me regala …? is a soft way to ask for small things, paid for or free.

examples.en: Could I have a still water?
Could I have a little bag?

grammar.trap: It doesn't mean you're asking for a gift; you still pay for what has a price. If in doubt, ¿me da …? works everywhere in Mexico.

vocabulary.en: Mexican sandwich in a crusty roll
spit-roasted marinated pork (tacos de pastor / al pastor)
coffee brewed with cinnamon and raw cane sugar
fruit or flower drink: horchata, jamaica, tamarindo
to contain (of food); to take away

pronunciation: Words ending in a vowel stress the next-to-last syllable: TA-co, TOR-ta, ce-BO-lla; a written accent marks the exceptions: li-MÓN, ja-MÓN.
h is always silent: horchata is 'or-CHA-ta'. ll sounds like y: cebolla is 'se-BO-ya', servilleta 'ser-vi-YE-ta'.

common_errors.wrong: Quiero tres tacos. (no greeting, no por favor)
common_errors.right: Buenas tardes. Me da tres tacos, por favor.
common_errors.why: Not wrong, but a bare quiero sounds abrupt to a stranger; me da … por favor is the polite norm.
Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a take un and el.
The filling follows the noun with de.
No article after con and sin when ordering.
Caliente means hot in temperature; spicy is picar / picante.

units.culture: At a taco stand you usually eat standing, pay at the end and tell the taquero how many you had; he keeps count too. Con todo means onion and cilantro; salsas and limes are on the counter, and limón in Mexico is the small green lime. Don't drink tap water: ask for agua natural (still), agua mineral (sparkling) or an agua fresca such as horchata or jamaica.
recycles: a1-04: Disculpe / Gracias / Con mucho gusto
units.evidence: At a food stand or café the learner orders with me da … por favor, says con todo or sin + ingredient, asks ¿pica? or ¿qué lleva?, answers ¿para aquí o para llevar?, and asks for small things politely with ¿me da …? or ¿me regala …?.

PCIC Saberes 1.4 (taquería; pay at the end at a taco stand), rewritten for Mexico

units.title: Numbers, prices and paying
units.can_do: Understand prices, ask how much, pay in cash or by card, sort out change, and give a phone number.
situations: paying at a small shop that has no change
a card terminal brought to the table
giving your number to a neighbour

frames.es: ¿Cuánto es? / ¿Cuánto le debo?

frames.es: ¿Aceptan tarjeta?

frames.en: Sorry, I don't have any change on me.
frames.note: Cambio = change, and also small notes and coins.

frames.es: ¿Me cobra, por favor?
frames.en: Can I pay, please?
frames.note: Lit. will you charge me; said to a waiter or at a counter.

frames.es: Aquí tiene su cambio.
frames.en: Here's your change.

frames.es: Mi celular es cincuenta y cinco, doce, treinta y cuatro …
frames.en: My mobile number is 55 12 34 …
frames.note: Ten digits, read in pairs.

grammar.explain: 16 to 19 and 21 to 29 are written as one word; from 31 on they're three words joined by y.

examples.es: treinta y cinco, cuarenta y ocho

grammar.trap: Sesenta (60) and setenta (70) are easy to confuse by ear; listen for the s or the t.

grammar.explain: Hundreds have their own forms, three of them irregular: quinientos (500), setecientos (700), novecientos (900); mil (1,000) needs no 'un'.
grammar.trap: Cien is exactly 100; from 101 it's ciento (ciento veinte). And it's mil, not 'un mil'.

grammar.point: ser for totals, costar for prices
grammar.explain: A total is son + amount; ¿cuánto cuesta? asks the price of one thing, ¿cuánto cuestan? of several.
grammar.trap: With an amount above one, use son: son ochenta pesos, not 'es ochenta pesos'.

grammar.explain: Mexicans use traer for what you're carrying right now.

examples.en: I don't have any change on me.

grammar.trap: Tener means having in general; for 'I don't have it on me', say no traigo.

grammar.point: Prices and phone numbers, Mexican style
grammar.explain: Prices use $ for pesos, a decimal point and a comma for thousands; phone numbers have ten digits, read in pairs.

examples.es: $85.50: ochenta y cinco pesos con cincuenta centavos
55 12 34 56 78: cincuenta y cinco, doce, treinta y cuatro, cincuenta y seis, setenta y ocho

grammar.trap: The $ sign on a price means pesos, not dollars, and the point and comma are the opposite of Spain's.

vocabulary.en: to bring; to have on you
a hundred (exactly); ciento before tens and units

pronunciation: Y joins tens and units in one breath: treinta y cinco sounds like 'trein-tai-sin-ko', cuarenta y ocho like 'kwa-ren-tai-o-cho'.
Dieciséis, veintidós and veintitrés are stressed on the last syllable (they carry an accent); seis/siete and sesenta/setenta differ in one sound, so say them clearly.

common_errors.why: Amounts above one take son.
Mil never takes un.
500, 700 and 900 are irregular.
From 101, it's ciento.
Several things take cuestan.

units.culture: Cash is still everyday money at markets, stalls, small shops and peseros, and change is often scarce: break 500 and 1,000 notes at supermarkets, convenience stores or the bank, and keep coins and 20s and 50s for small purchases. In restaurants the waiter brings the card terminal to the table, so your card doesn't leave your sight. A tip of about 10–15% is normal in sit-down restaurants.
units.evidence: The learner asks ¿cuánto es? or ¿cuánto le debo?, understands a spoken price in the hundreds, asks ¿aceptan tarjeta?, deals with a change problem (¿tiene cambio de …?, no traigo cambio), asks for the bill with ¿me cobra?, and gives a ten-digit number in pairs.

WP §6.3 (efectivo, cambio, ¿aceptan tarjeta?, propina)

grammar.explain: ¿Tiene …? asks the shopkeeper whether they have something; ¿hay …? asks whether there's any (here, today).
grammar.trap: Hay never changes and never takes el or la: hay leche, hay unos cuadernos, not 'hay la leche'.

grammar.point: este / ese / aquel with acá / allá
grammar.explain: Este is near you (acá), ese is near the other person or a bit away, aquel is far off (allá); they can stand alone for 'this one' and 'that one', and agree with the thing (esta, esa).

examples.en: Can I have that one, please? (a feminine thing)

grammar.trap: There's no word for 'one': say este, not 'este uno'. Mexicans use acá and allá a lot, alongside aquí and ahí; allí is rare in speech.

grammar.explain: Nomás is the everyday Mexican word for 'just' or 'only', and it's neutral, not slang.
grammar.trap: Don't confuse it with no más (no more): nomás eso means 'just that'.

grammar.point: ya no = no longer, none left
grammar.explain: Ya no (+ verb) means 'not any more'; shopkeepers use it when something has run out.
grammar.trap: Ya alone means 'already' or 'now'; it's ya no that means 'not any more'.

grammar.point: me lo llevo as a chunk
grammar.explain: 'I'll take it': lo for a masculine thing, la for a feminine one, los or las for several. Object pronouns are explained at A2.
grammar.trap: Match lo or la to the thing you're buying, not to yourself.

vocabulary.en: shop; la tiendita = the corner shop
round sweet bun with a shell pattern

pronunciation: h is silent and hue- sounds like 'we': hay is 'ai', huevos is 'we-bos'.
Words ending in a vowel, n or s stress the next-to-last syllable (TIEN-da, CO-pias, PI-las); others the last; a written accent marks a break in the rule: pa-pe-le-RÍ-a, pa-na-de-RÍ-a, a-CÁ, a-LLÁ.

common_errors.why: Hay never takes el or la.
Spanish has no word for 'one' after este or ese.
To ask the shopkeeper, use tener; hay doesn't take a person.
Cuaderno is masculine, so lo.
Several things take cuestan.

units.culture: The tiendita on the corner sells a bit of everything and often gets to know its regulars. In most bakeries you serve yourself: take a tray (charola) and tongs (pinzas), choose your bread, and take it to the till to be bagged and charged. Papelerías do copies, printing and scans, which you'll need for any paperwork.
recycles: a1-06: ¿Cuánto es? / ¿Cuánto cuesta? / prices in pesos
a1-04: Disculpe / Nada más estoy viendo
units.evidence: The learner asks a shop whether they have something (¿tiene …?) or whether there is any (¿hay …?), points with este / ese / el de allá when the word is missing, understands ya no hay, answers ¿algo más? with es todo or nomás eso, and closes with me lo / la llevo.
sources: ELE L6 (hay, este/ese, ¿tienen…?, me lo llevo)
EeM U9 (este / ese / aquel), U15 (¿algo más?, no me queda ninguna)
PCIC Gram. A1 (hay, demonstratives); Tác. A1 1.3 ([Hispanoamérica] acá / allá); Gram. B1–B2 ([Hispanoamérica] no más; moved down)
PCIC Saberes 1.11 (tiendita, panadería with tray and tongs, papelería), rewritten for Mexico

units.title: At the market
units.can_do: Buy fruit, vegetables and tortillas by weight, ask the price per kilo, taste before buying, and follow the stallholder's patter.

frames.es: ¿Qué le damos, güera?
frames.en: What can we get you?
frames.note: Güera to a woman, güero to a man; friendly market talk.

frames.es: ¿A cómo está el kilo de jitomate?
frames.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?
frames.note: Also ¿a cómo el kilo? Jitomate is the red tomato; in central Mexico tomate is the green tomatillo (in the north tomate can mean the red one).

frames.es: Deme medio kilo, por favor.
frames.en: Give me half a kilo, please.

frames.es: Un kilo de tortillas, por favor.
frames.en: A kilo of tortillas, please.

frames.es: ¿Me da a probar?
frames.en: Can I try some?

frames.es: Están bien dulces, ándele.
frames.en: They're really sweet, go on.

frames.es: Ahí le va su pilón.
frames.en: There's a little extra for you.

frames.es: ¿Quién sigue?
frames.en: Who's next?

frames.es: ¿Cuánto le doy?
frames.en: How much do I owe you?
frames.note: Lit. how much do I give you.

model_exchanges.situation: At a vegetable stall

lines.speaker: vendor
lines.es: ¿Qué le damos, güera?
lines.en: What can we get you?

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.en: Good morning. How much is a kilo of tomatoes?

lines.speaker: vendor
lines.es: A treinta.
lines.en: Thirty.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Deme medio kilo, por favor. ¿Y los aguacates?
lines.en: Give me half a kilo, please. And the avocados?

lines.speaker: vendor
lines.es: ¿Algo más?
lines.en: Anything else?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Es todo. ¿Cuánto le doy?
lines.en: That's all. How much do I owe you?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Me da a probar el mango?
lines.en: Can I try the mango?

lines.speaker: vendor
lines.es: Sí, pruebe. Están bien dulces, ándele.
lines.en: Sure, try it. They're really sweet, go on.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Mmm, sí. Deme un kilo, por favor.

lines.speaker: vendor

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.en: Thank you!

lines.es: ¿Quién sigue?

lines.en: Me. A kilo of tortillas, please.

lines.speaker: worker

lines.en: No, that's all, thanks.

grammar.explain: Weights and amounts are followed by de + the food: un kilo de, medio kilo de, un cuarto de, doscientos gramos de.
grammar.trap: Medio has no un before it: medio kilo, not 'un medio kilo'. At a stall, medio on its own means half a kilo.

grammar.point: estar a for prices that change
grammar.explain: ¿A cómo está …? asks the price of something sold by weight, whose price changes from day to day.

examples.es: ¿A cómo está el kilo de jitomate?
examples.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes?

grammar.trap: Use it at markets for produce; for a fixed price in a shop, ask ¿cuánto cuesta?.

grammar.point: deme, pruebe: usted commands as chunks
grammar.explain: Deme (give me) and pruebe (try) are usted commands; at a market they're polite enough on their own.

examples.en: Tell me. / What can I get you?

grammar.trap: With a friend it's dame; with a stallholder say deme or ¿me da …?.

grammar.explain: Mexicans use bien before an adjective to mean 'really' or 'very'.
grammar.trap: This bien means 'really', not 'well': bien caro is 'very expensive', not 'well priced'.

grammar.explain: Stallholders call customers güero / güera, marchante or joven to catch their attention and build friendliness.

examples.en: Come on in, my dear customer.

grammar.trap: Güero / güera is sales talk, not a comment on your looks, and you don't need to answer it; just say what you want.

vocabulary.en: a little extra the vendor adds for free
regular customer; how vendors address you (marchanta for a woman)

pronunciation: Many market words come from Nahuatl and are stressed like Spanish words: ji-to-MA-te, a-gua-CA-te, e-LO-te, CHI-le, TIAN-guis.
Gua and güe start with a soft 'gw': a-GUA-ca-te, GÜE-ro. The dots in güe tell you to pronounce the u.

common_errors.why: Medio takes no article.

common_errors.wrong: ¿A cómo está el kilo de tomate? (wanting red tomatoes)
common_errors.right: ¿A cómo está el kilo de jitomate?
common_errors.why: In central Mexico tomate is the green tomatillo.

common_errors.wrong: Dame un kilo. (to an older stallholder)
common_errors.right: Deme un kilo. / ¿Me da un kilo?
common_errors.why: Stallholders get usted.
Quantities need de.

units.culture: Markets run on relationships: buy from the same stalls and you become a marchante, with better fruit picked for you and a pilón, a small free extra. Vendors are happy to let you taste (¿me da a probar?) and will ask whether you want avocados for today or for later. Bargaining is fine at a tianguis and at craft stalls, but not for everyday food at fixed-price stalls. Bring your own bag, and buy tortillas by the kilo, hot from the tortillería.
units.evidence: At a stall the learner asks ¿a cómo está el kilo de …?, orders by weight with medio kilo / un kilo / un cuarto de, asks to taste, understands the vendor's patter (¿qué le damos?, ¿algo más?, ahí le va su pilón, ¿quién sigue?) and pays.
sources: EeM U15 (market-stall dialogue, quantities; A2, moved to A1 per D5)
PCIC Gram. B1 (estar a: ¿a cómo está el kilo?; moved down); NG A2 2.6 and NE A2 12.3 (medio kilo, un cuarto, gramos, adapted)
PCIC Saberes 1.11 (mercado, marchantes, pilón, ¿me da a probar?, ¿quién sigue?; bargaining only at tianguis and crafts), rewritten for Mexico
WP §6.5 (jitomate, tomate verde, elote, limón, kilo/medio/cuarto)

units.title: Asking the way
units.can_do: Ask where something is and follow simple directions given in blocks, corners and landmarks.
situations: finding a stop or a station

frames.es: Disculpe, ¿dónde está el metro?
frames.en: Excuse me, where's the metro?

frames.es: ¿Hay un cajero por aquí?
frames.en: Is there an ATM around here?

frames.es: ¿Dónde queda el mercado?
frames.en: Where's the market?
frames.note: Quedar = to be (located); very common for places.

frames.es: ¿Qué tan lejos está?
frames.en: How far is it?

frames.es: Está a dos cuadras.
frames.en: It's two blocks away.

frames.es: Siga derecho y dé vuelta a la derecha.
frames.en: Go straight on and turn right.

frames.es: Está enfrente de la farmacia, en la esquina.
frames.en: It's opposite the pharmacy, on the corner.

frames.es: ¿Derecho dos cuadras y a la derecha?
frames.en: Straight on two blocks and then right?
frames.note: Repeat the directions back to check you've got them.

frames.es: Gracias, muy amable.
frames.en: Thanks, that's very kind.

model_exchanges.situation: Looking for an ATM

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, ¿hay un cajero por aquí?
lines.en: Excuse me, is there an ATM around here?

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.es: Sí, hay uno en el súper. Siga derecho dos cuadras y dé vuelta a la izquierda.
lines.en: Yes, there's one in the supermarket. Go straight on two blocks and turn left.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Derecho dos cuadras y a la izquierda?
lines.en: Straight on two blocks and left?

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.es: Ándele, ahí está, en la esquina.
lines.en: That's it, it's right there, on the corner.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Gracias, muy amable.
lines.en: Thanks, that's very kind.

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.es: De nada.
lines.en: You're welcome.

model_exchanges.situation: Asking an older woman where the market is

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, señora, ¿dónde queda el mercado?
lines.en: Excuse me, madam, where's the market?

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: Está cerca, a cinco minutos. Cruce la avenida y tome la primera calle a la derecha.
lines.en: It's close, five minutes away. Cross the avenue and take the first street on the right.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Me lo puede repetir más despacio?
lines.en: Could you say that again more slowly?

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: Sí. Cruce la avenida… y la primera a la derecha. El mercado está enfrente de la iglesia.
lines.en: Yes. Cross the avenue… and the first on the right. The market is opposite the church.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Muchas gracias.
lines.en: Thank you very much.

lines.es: Joven, ¿dónde está el metro?

lines.speaker: young man

lines.en: The metro? It's a bit far, about fifteen minutes on foot.

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.en: Is there a bus stop?

lines.speaker: young man

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Gracias.
lines.en: Thanks.

grammar.point: estar for location, hay for whether one exists
grammar.explain: Use estar (or quedar) to ask where a known place is, and hay to ask whether there is one at all.

examples.en: Is there a pharmacy around here?

examples.es: El cajero está en el súper.
examples.en: The ATM is in the supermarket.

grammar.trap: The location of a place never takes ser: '¿dónde es el metro?' is wrong (events are different: ¿dónde es la fiesta?). And hay goes with un/una: hay un cajero, not 'hay el cajero'.

grammar.explain: Distance is given with a: a dos cuadras, a cinco minutos.
grammar.trap: Don't leave out the a: 'está dos cuadras' is wrong.

grammar.explain: People give directions with usted commands: siga (keep going), dé vuelta (turn), cruce (cross), tome (take).

examples.es: Cruce la avenida y tome la primera a la derecha.
examples.en: Cross the avenue and take the first on the right.

grammar.trap: You only need to understand these now. Dar vuelta is the everyday Mexican 'turn', and derecho, not recto, is 'straight on'.

grammar.explain: Enfrente de (opposite), al lado de (next to), en la esquina (on the corner), a la derecha / a la izquierda (on the right / left), derecho (straight on).

examples.es: Está al lado de la farmacia.
Está en la esquina, a la derecha.
examples.en: It's on the corner, on the right.

grammar.trap: Derecho (straight on) and derecha (right) differ by one vowel; a la derecha is 'on the right'.

grammar.explain: De + el becomes del, and a + el becomes al; la never contracts.
grammar.trap: 'Enfrente de el mercado' is wrong; but enfrente de la farmacia stays as it is.

vocabulary.en: right (a la derecha = on the right)
left (a la izquierda = on the left)

pronunciation: Derecho and derecha differ only in the final vowel: keep the o and the a pure and clear, or people won't know whether to go straight on or turn right.
A single r between vowels is a quick tap, like the tt in American 'butter': derecho, para, cuadra. R at the start of a word and rr are rolled: rápido, carro, Reforma.

common_errors.why: Location takes estar, not ser.

common_errors.right: ¿Hay un cajero por aquí? / ¿Dónde está el cajero?
common_errors.why: Hay goes with un/una; a specific place takes está.
De + el contracts to del.
Distance needs a.

units.culture: Directions in Mexico are given in cuadras (blocks) and landmarks (the church, the pharmacy, the convenience store) more than street names. Repeating the directions back is normal and helps. Some people would rather give you directions than say they don't know, so if you're unsure, ask a second person. Thank with 'muy amable'.
recycles: a1-02: ¿Me lo puede repetir? / Más despacio
units.evidence: The learner asks where a place is with ¿dónde está / queda …? or whether there's one nearby with ¿hay un … por aquí?, asks how far, follows directions given in cuadras and landmarks, repeats them back to check, and thanks the person.
sources: EeM U6 (¿cómo se va a…?), U8 (asking and giving directions; the receptionist and the learner's read-back), U14 (¿podría decirme…?)
ELE L7 (ser vs estar for places), L8 (prepositions of place; del); grammar summary (the one directions example)
PCIC NG A1 3.3–3.6 (cerca / lejos, derecha; todo recto → derecho); NG A2 (girar → dar vuelta; coger la primera → tome la primera)
7K ch.6 (muy amable)
WP §6.11 (cuadra, esquina, banqueta, glorieta, ¿dónde queda?, ¿qué tan lejos?)

units.title: Times, days and opening hours
units.can_do: Ask and tell the time, ask when somewhere opens, understand that "hasta" can mean "not until", and fix a time to meet.
situations: checking when a shop or an office opens

frames.es: ¿Qué horas son? — Son las cinco y media.
frames.en: What time is it? — It's half past five.
frames.note: ¿Qué hora es? is also correct; ¿qué horas son? is the everyday Mexican question.

frames.es: Son veinte para las ocho. / Es cuarto para las tres.
frames.en: It's twenty to eight. / It's quarter to three.

frames.es: ¿A qué hora abren? / ¿A qué hora cierran?
frames.en: What time do you open? / What time do you close?

frames.es: Abren hasta las diez.
frames.en: They don't open until ten.
frames.note: In Mexico hasta + time often means 'not until'.

frames.es: De lunes a viernes, de nueve a seis.
frames.en: Monday to Friday, nine to six.

frames.es: Mañana en la mañana.
frames.en: Tomorrow morning.

frames.es: ¿Nos vemos el sábado a las cinco? — ¡Sale!
frames.en: Shall we meet on Saturday at five? — Sure!

frames.es: Ahorita vengo.
frames.en: I'll be right back.
frames.note: Ahorita can mean now, in a bit, or later.

model_exchanges.situation: Checking when an office opens

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Buenos días. ¿A qué hora abren?
lines.en: Good morning. What time do you open?

lines.speaker: guard
lines.es: Abrimos hasta las diez.
lines.en: We don't open until ten.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Hasta las diez? ¿Y qué horas son?
lines.en: Not until ten? And what time is it now?

lines.speaker: guard
lines.es: Son las nueve y veinte.
lines.en: It's twenty past nine.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Ah, bueno. ¿Y a qué hora cierran?
lines.en: OK. And what time do you close?

lines.speaker: guard
lines.es: A las seis, de lunes a viernes.
lines.en: At six, Monday to Friday.

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: ¿Quieres ir al tianguis el sábado?
lines.en: Do you want to go to the street market on Saturday?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Sí! ¿A qué hora?
lines.en: Yes! What time?

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: ¿En la mañana? ¿A las diez?
lines.en: In the morning? At ten?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Sale! Nos vemos el sábado a las diez.
lines.en: Great! See you on Saturday at ten.

lines.speaker: neighbour

lines.en: OK. Down here, at the door.

model_exchanges.situation: Telling a shopkeeper you'll be back

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, ahorita vengo. Voy al cajero.
lines.en: Excuse me, I'll be right back. I'm going to the ATM.

lines.speaker: shopkeeper
lines.es: Sí, ándele. ¿Le aparto el pan?
lines.en: Sure, go ahead. Shall I put the bread aside for you?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, por favor. Un momentito.
lines.en: Yes, please. Just a moment.

lines.speaker: shopkeeper
lines.es: Sale.
lines.en: OK.

grammar.point: ser for the time: es la una, son las dos
grammar.explain: Time uses ser with la or las: es la una for one o'clock, son las … for every other hour; add minutes with y, or count down with para.
grammar.trap: Es la una is singular; 'son la una' is wrong. Mexicans usually count down with para (veinte para las ocho); menos (las ocho menos veinte) is understood but sounds less local.

grammar.explain: At a time is a las …; on a day is el + day, with no preposition; los + day means every week.
grammar.trap: No 'en' before days: el lunes means 'on Monday'. Days and months are written with a small letter.

grammar.point: hasta = 'not until' in Mexico; de … a … for ranges
grammar.explain: In Mexico, hasta + a time often means 'not until'; a range of times or days is de … a ….

examples.es: El doctor llega hasta las cuatro.
examples.en: The doctor isn't in until four.

examples.es: De lunes a viernes, de nueve a seis.
examples.en: Monday to Friday, nine to six.

grammar.trap: Abren hasta las diez doesn't mean 'open until ten'; it means they open at ten. If in doubt, ask ¿a qué hora abren?.

grammar.point: en la mañana / en la tarde / en la noche
grammar.explain: Mexicans say en la mañana (in the morning), en la tarde, en la noche; mañana also means tomorrow.
grammar.trap: Por la mañana is also correct and understood, but en la mañana is the everyday Mexican form.

grammar.point: The present for plans; saying yes
grammar.explain: A plan for later can be asked in the present tense (¿nos vemos …?), and Mexicans agree with sale, va, órale or está bien.
grammar.trap: Vale is Spain's 'OK'; in Mexico say sale or va.

grammar.point: ahorita and al rato: elastic time
grammar.explain: Ahorita can mean right now, in a little while or later; al rato means later on.

examples.en: I'll do it in a bit.

grammar.trap: Don't read ahorita as a firm 'immediately'. If you need a time, ask ¿a qué hora?.

vocabulary.en: quarter (y cuarto = quarter past; cuarto para = quarter to)
Monday (also martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo)
January (also febrero, marzo, abril, mayo, junio, julio, agosto, septiembre, octubre, noviembre, diciembre)
right now; in a little while; later

pronunciation: A final s links to the next vowel, and h is silent: las ocho sounds like 'la-so-cho', ¿qué horas son? like 'ke-o-ras-son'.
Stress the days correctly: MIÉR-co-les, SÁ-ba-do, DO-min-go; lunes, martes, jueves and viernes end in s and don't change in the plural (los lunes).

common_errors.why: One o'clock is singular.
Days take el, no preposition.

common_errors.wrong: Abren hasta las diez = 'open until ten'
common_errors.right: Abren hasta las diez = 'they don't open until ten'
common_errors.why: In Mexico hasta + time often marks the start.
Tiempo is weather or time as duration, not clock time.
Vale is Spain's word.

units.culture: Shops in Mexican cities generally stay open through the middle of the day, and convenience stores open long hours. Appointments with doctors, offices and banks start more or less on time, but social plans are looser: arriving a bit late to a party at someone's home is normal, and invitations rarely have an end time. Ahorita is famous for its elasticity; Mexicans themselves joke about it.
units.evidence: The learner asks and tells the time (¿qué horas son?, son las …), asks when a place opens and closes, understands hasta + time as 'not until', arranges a day and time with ¿nos vemos el … a las …?, and agrees with sale or va.
sources: ELE L10 (the time, opening hours, days, months; Mexican cuarto para, ¿qué horas son?), L13 (de … a, desde … hasta)
EeM U2 (telling the time; Mexican para), U7 (arranging to meet)
PCIC NG A1 4.1 (¿qué hora es? → ¿qué horas son?; [Hispanoamérica] veinte para las diez; en la mañana); Gram. A2 15.3.1 ([México] hasta = not until; D14); Func. A2 4.16 (vale → sale / va)
7K ch.7 (social time is flexible) and §5–6 gaps (ahorita, al rato)
WP §6.4 (cuarto para las nueve, ahorita, al rato)

units.title: Getting around
units.can_do: Take buses, peseros, the metro and taxis: ask where a bus goes, ask the fare, get off where you want, and choose a safe taxi.
functions: tell a driver where to stop
situations: getting a safe taxi at night

frames.es: ¿Este camión pasa por el centro?
frames.en: Does this bus go through the centre?
frames.note: Camión = city bus in everyday speech; autobús is understood, and is the usual word for long-distance coaches.

frames.es: ¿Cuánto es el pasaje?
frames.en: How much is the fare?

frames.es: ¡Bajan! / En la esquina, por favor.
frames.en: Getting off! / At the corner, please.
frames.note: On a pesero (minibus), call out ¡bajan! before your stop.

frames.es: ¿Qué línea tomo para ir al centro?
frames.en: Which line do I take to get to the centre?

frames.es: ¿Dónde me bajo para ir al mercado?
frames.en: Where do I get off for the market?

frames.es: ¿Me pide un taxi de sitio, por favor?
frames.en: Could you call me a taxi from the rank, please?

frames.es: Aquí está bien, gracias.
frames.en: Here's fine, thanks.

frames.es: Ya estoy afuera, en un carro gris.
frames.en: I'm outside, in a grey car.
frames.note: What a ride-app driver may say or text.

frames.es: Voy en metro. / Voy caminando.
frames.en: I'm going by metro. / I'm walking.

model_exchanges.situation: In the metro

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, ¿qué línea tomo para ir al centro?

lines.speaker: metro worker
lines.es: Tome la línea dos y bájese en la tercera estación.
lines.en: Take line two and get off at the third station.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿En la tercera?
lines.en: At the third one?

lines.speaker: metro worker
lines.es: Ándele, la tercera.
lines.en: That's right, the third.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Gracias.
lines.en: Thanks.

model_exchanges.situation: Asking for a safe taxi at night

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, ¿me pide un taxi de sitio, por favor?
lines.en: Excuse me, could you call me a taxi from the rank, please?

lines.speaker: waiter
lines.es: Sí, cómo no. ¿A dónde va?
lines.en: Yes, of course. Where are you going?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Al centro.
lines.en: To the centre.

lines.speaker: waiter
lines.es: Ahorita llega, como en diez minutos.
lines.en: It'll be here soon, in about ten minutes.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Muchas gracias.
lines.en: Thank you very much.

grammar.point: tomar for buses, the metro and taxis
grammar.explain: To take a bus, the metro or a taxi is tomar.
grammar.trap: Never use coger in Mexico: in Spain it means 'take', but in Mexico it's vulgar. Always tomar.

grammar.explain: Say how you travel with en + vehicle, and caminando for on foot.
grammar.trap: Not 'en pie' or 'en caminando'; just caminando (a pie is understood too).

grammar.explain: ¿Pasa por …? asks whether a bus goes through a place; getting on and off are subirse and bajarse, with me, se.

examples.en: Does this bus go past the market?

grammar.trap: Keep the me: me bajo aquí, not 'bajo aquí'. You'll hear the usted commands súbase and bájese.

grammar.explain: Ir is going away from where you are; venir is coming towards where the speaker is.

examples.en: Are you coming to my place?

grammar.trap: When someone calls you, 'I'm coming' is ¡ya voy!, not 'ya vengo' (which means 'I'm on my way back').

vocabulary.en: minibus that stops anywhere on its route (also combi, micro)
rapid bus with its own lane and stations
taxi from a rank or called by phone (the safe option)
to take (a bus, the metro, a taxi)

pronunciation: Indigenous place names: tl is said together, as in the middle of 'atlas', even at the start of a word (Tlalpan, Tlatelolco); x sounds like j in México and Oaxaca, like s in Xochimilco, and like 'sh' in Maya names such as Uxmal.
Camión is stressed on the last syllable, as the accent shows: ca-MIÓN, not 'CA-mion'. Stress can change meaning: ca-MI-no (I walk) vs ca-mi-NÓ (he or she walked).

common_errors.why: Coger is vulgar in Mexico.
On foot is caminando (or a pie).
Bajarse needs me.
Moving towards the other person is ir in Spanish.
'Goes through' is pasar por; pasa el centro means it goes past and beyond it.

units.culture: Most cities run on camiones and peseros: you flag them anywhere on the route, pay the driver (often in coins), and call out ¡bajan! or 'en la esquina, por favor' to get off. Mexico City's metro is cheap and busy, with women-and-children-only carriages at the front, and the Metrobús is a fast bus with its own lanes and stations. At night, take a taxi de sitio (from a rank or called for you) or a ride app rather than hailing a taxi in the street.
recycles: a1-09: ¿Dónde está …? / a la derecha / en la esquina
units.evidence: The learner asks whether a bus goes through a place (¿pasa por …?), asks the fare, asks where to get off and says ¡bajan! or 'en la esquina, por favor', asks which metro line to take, asks for a taxi de sitio, and says how they get around with tomar / ir en / caminando.
sources: ELE L13 (transport, ir vs venir; Mexican tomar, never coger)
EeM U6 (transport information at the metro; Mexican boleto, transbordar)
PCIC NG A2 3.5 (pasar por: el camión no pasa por el centro; subir, bajar); NE A1–A2 14.3 (travel: tomar, never coger)
PCIC Saberes 1.13.4 (Metro, Metrobús, pesero and ¡bajan!, taxi libre vs de sitio vs apps), rewritten for Mexico
7K ch.1 (Nahuatl place names), ch.2 (taxi de sitio)
WP §6.11 (camión, parada, pasaje, ¡bajan!, en la esquina, por favor)

units.title: Your home
units.can_do: Describe where you live, find your way round a flat, and deal with the basics: water, the landlord, the bathroom.
functions: say what there is and where
ask where something is in a home
say something is missing or not working

frames.es: Rento un departamento en la colonia …
frames.en: I rent a flat in the … neighbourhood.
frames.note: Depa for short.

frames.es: Está en el tercer piso.
frames.en: It's on the third floor.
frames.note: The ground floor is la planta baja; primer piso is usually the floor above it.

frames.es: Tiene dos recámaras y una cocina chiquita.
frames.en: It has two bedrooms and a small kitchen.

frames.es: ¿Dónde está el baño?
frames.en: Where's the bathroom?

frames.es: No hay agua caliente.
frames.en: There's no hot water.

frames.es: Mi casero vive abajo.
frames.en: My landlord lives downstairs.
frames.note: Mi casera for a woman; also el dueño, la dueña.

frames.es: El agua de la llave no se toma.
frames.en: You don't drink the tap water.

frames.es: ¿Me deja dos garrafones, por favor?
frames.en: Could you leave me two jugs of water, please?
frames.note: To the water delivery; a garrafón is a 20-litre jug of purified water.

model_exchanges.situation: Showing a friend your flat (tú)

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: ¡Qué bonito tu depa! ¿Cuántas recámaras tiene?
lines.en: What a nice flat! How many bedrooms does it have?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Tiene dos recámaras y un baño.
lines.en: It has two bedrooms and a bathroom.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: ¿Y la cocina?
lines.en: And the kitchen?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Está allá, al lado de la sala. Es chiquita.
lines.en: It's over there, next to the living room. It's small.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: ¿Hay azotea?
lines.en: Is there a roof terrace?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, arriba. Ahí está el tinaco.
lines.en: Yes, upstairs. That's where the water tank is.

model_exchanges.situation: The water delivery

lines.speaker: delivery man
lines.es: ¡El agua!
lines.en: Water!

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Joven! ¿Me deja dos garrafones, por favor?
lines.en: Excuse me! Could you leave me two jugs, please?

lines.speaker: delivery man
lines.es: Sí. ¿En qué piso?
lines.en: Sure. Which floor?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: En el tercero.
lines.en: The third.

lines.speaker: delivery man
lines.es: Sale, ahorita se los subo.
lines.en: OK, I'll bring them up now.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Gracias.
lines.en: Thanks.

model_exchanges.situation: Telling the landlord there's no hot water (usted)

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Buenas tardes, don Arturo. Disculpe, no hay agua caliente.
lines.en: Good afternoon, don Arturo. Sorry, there's no hot water.

lines.speaker: landlord
lines.es: ¿No hay? A ver… ¿Hay gas?
lines.en: There isn't? Let's see… Is there gas?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: No sé.
lines.en: I don't know.

lines.speaker: landlord
lines.es: Ahorita subo a ver el bóiler.
lines.en: I'll come up and look at the water heater.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Muchas gracias, muy amable.
lines.en: Thank you very much, that's very kind.

grammar.point: hay vs está in a home
grammar.explain: Hay says what there is (with un, una or a number); está says where a particular thing is (with el, la, mi).

examples.es: Hay un baño y dos recámaras.
examples.en: There's a bathroom and two bedrooms.
The bathroom is at the back.

grammar.trap: Not 'hay el baño' or 'el baño hay': use hay for 'there is', está for 'it's (located)'.

grammar.explain: Primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto … décimo; primero and tercero drop the -o before a masculine noun.

examples.en: I live on the first floor.

grammar.trap: Say el tercer piso, not 'el tercero piso'. And check which floor people mean: in Mexico la planta baja is the ground floor and the first piso is usually the one above it.

grammar.point: tener for what a home has
grammar.explain: To say what a flat has, use tiene, just as in English 'it has'.
grammar.trap: Don't use es for what a flat has: 'es dos recámaras' is wrong.

grammar.explain: Possessives go before the noun and take -s in the plural; su can mean his, her, their or your (usted).
grammar.trap: No article with them: mi casa, not 'la mi casa'. When su is unclear, Mexicans say la casa de él / de ella.

grammar.point: The diminutive for size and warmth
grammar.explain: -ito / -ita makes things small and also sounds friendly; after -e or a consonant it's often -cito.
grammar.trap: A diminutive isn't a complaint: una cocina chiquita is neutral, even affectionate.

vocabulary.en: flat roof (used for water tanks and drying washing)
floor, storey; floor (the ground you walk on)

pronunciation: In recámara the first r is rolled (it starts the word) and the second is a quick tap: re-CÁ-ma-ra. The same tap is in tercero and departamento.
Written accents show unexpected stress: re-CÁ-ma-ra, BÓI-ler, ga-rra-FÓN; caliente and cocina follow the normal rule and need none.

common_errors.why: A particular thing's location takes está.

common_errors.wrong: Vivo en un piso. (meaning a flat)
common_errors.why: In Mexico piso means floor.
Tercero drops the -o before a masculine noun.
Not wrong (alquilar is correct and understood), but rentar is the everyday Mexican verb: se renta, rento un depa.
Terrateniente means a big landowner.

units.culture: Don't drink tap water in Mexico: households buy garrafones of purified water, delivered by trucks or bicycles that call out in the street. Water is stored in a tinaco on the roof (and sometimes a cistern), and hot water comes from a gas water heater; if the gas runs out, so does the hot water. Gas comes in tanks delivered by trucks you'll hear in the street. Most homes have no central heating.
recycles: a1-03: Vivo en la colonia … / casero / vecino
a1-09: al lado de / allá / hay vs está
units.evidence: The learner describes their home with tiene + rooms, says which floor it's on, asks where something is with ¿dónde está …?, reports a problem with no hay …, and orders water or asks the landlord for help politely.
sources: ELE L8 (the home: hay vs está, prepositions; Mexican depa, rentar, recámara, regadera)
EeM U4 (rooms, ordinals, hay / está)
PCIC NE A1–A2 10 (housing, adapted: rentar un depa, casero, ¿hay agua caliente?); Gram. A1 (ordinals)
PCIC Saberes 1.9 (garrafón, tinaco, gas, no tap water), rewritten for Mexico
WP §6.7 (casero, not terrateniente; planta baja / primer piso; garrafón, tinaco)

units.title: Likes, food and the weather
units.can_do: Say what you like, agree or disagree with someone's likes, and make small talk about the food and the weather.
functions: say what you like and love
situations: a neighbour's comment on the rain
talking about food with someone you just met

frames.es: Me gusta mucho la comida de aquí.
frames.en: I really like the food here.

frames.es: Me encantan los tamales.
frames.en: I love tamales.

frames.es: A mí también. / A mí no. / A mí tampoco.
frames.en: Me too. / Not me. / Me neither.

frames.es: ¿Te gusta México? — ¡Sí, mucho!
frames.en: Do you like Mexico? — Yes, a lot!
frames.note: With usted: ¿Le gusta…?

frames.es: ¡Qué rico!
frames.en: How delicious!

frames.es: ¡Hace mucho calor hoy!
frames.en: It's really hot today!

frames.es: Parece que va a llover, ¿verdad?
frames.en: Looks like it's going to rain, doesn't it?

frames.es: Es temporada de lluvias: llueve todas las tardes.
frames.en: It's the rainy season: it rains every afternoon.

frames.es: ¿A poco no te gusta el picante?
frames.en: You mean you don't like spicy food?

model_exchanges.situation: Chatting about the weather while waiting in line (usted)

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: ¡Qué calor hace hoy!, ¿verdad?
lines.en: It's so hot today, isn't it?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, hace mucho calor.
lines.en: Yes, it's really hot.

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: Pero parece que va a llover en la tarde.
lines.en: But it looks like it's going to rain this afternoon.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Otra vez?
lines.en: Again?

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: Sí, es temporada de lluvias: llueve todas las tardes.
lines.en: Yes, it's the rainy season: it rains every afternoon.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Ah, por eso.
lines.en: Ah, that's why.

model_exchanges.situation: Talking about food with someone you just met (tú)

lines.speaker: Paco
lines.es: ¿Te gusta la comida de aquí?
lines.en: Do you like the food here?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Sí, mucho! Me encantan los tamales.
lines.en: Yes, a lot! I love tamales.

lines.speaker: Paco
lines.es: A mí también. ¿Y el mole?
lines.en: Me too. And mole?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me gusta, pero pica un poco.
lines.en: I like it, but it's a bit spicy.

lines.speaker: Paco
lines.es: ¿A poco no te gusta el picante?
lines.en: You mean you don't like spicy food?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Poquito sí, mucho no.
lines.en: A little, yes; a lot, no.

model_exchanges.situation: A neighbour asks how you like it here (usted)

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: ¿Le gusta México?
lines.en: Do you like Mexico?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, me encanta. Me gusta mucho la gente.
lines.en: Yes, I love it. I really like the people.

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: ¿Y el clima?
lines.en: And the weather?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: En la mañana hace frío y en la tarde hace calor.
lines.en: In the morning it's cold and in the afternoon it's hot.

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: Así es aquí.
lines.en: That's how it is here.

grammar.point: gustar and encantar with me, te, le
grammar.explain: Me gusta means 'it pleases me': gusta with one thing or a verb, gustan with several; encantar (to love) works the same way.

examples.es: Me gusta la comida de aquí.

grammar.trap: The thing liked decides gusta or gustan, and it keeps its article: me gustan los tacos, not 'me gusta tacos' or 'yo gusto tacos'. Encantar already means 'love', so you don't need mucho (though you'll hear me encanta mucho).

grammar.point: a mí también / tampoco / sí / no
grammar.explain: To agree or disagree about likes, answer with a mí + también, tampoco, sí or no.

examples.es: —No me gusta el frío. —A mí tampoco.
—No me gusta el picante. —A mí sí.

grammar.trap: After a negative, agreeing is tampoco, not también.

grammar.point: hace + weather; llueve; va a llover
grammar.explain: Most weather uses hace (hace calor, hace frío, hace sol); rain is llueve, and va a llover is 'it's going to rain'.
grammar.trap: Don't say 'es caliente' or 'está caliente' for the weather; caliente is for food, water or objects. For yourself, say tengo calor.

grammar.explain: Muy goes before an adjective or adverb; mucho goes after a verb or before a noun.

examples.en: It's very hot. (lit. it makes much heat)

grammar.trap: 'Mucho bonito' is wrong: say muy bonito.

grammar.explain: Add ¿verdad? or ¿no? to a statement to invite agreement, like English 'isn't it?'.
grammar.trap: The tag never changes, whatever the verb: no need to match it like English 'doesn't it / isn't it'.

grammar.explain: Mexicans use ¿a poco …? to show surprise or disbelief: 'you mean …?', 'really?'.

examples.en: You mean you don't like it?

grammar.trap: It's friendly surprise, not a challenge; answer it like a normal question.

vocabulary.form: me gusta, me gustan, te gusta, le gusta

vocabulary.en: food; the main meal of the day, eaten around 2–4 p.m.

pronunciation: Gusta and gustan differ only in the final n: let it be heard, because it tells people whether you like one thing or several.
ll in llueve and lluvia sounds like y: 'YUE-be', 'YU-bia'. And v sounds like b: lluvia, verdad.

common_errors.why: Gustar works like 'please': the tacos please me.
Plural thing liked → gustan, with the article.
Agreeing with a negative takes tampoco.
Weather uses hacer, and calor is a noun, so mucho.
One thing loved takes encanta; several take encantan.

units.culture: Food is the easiest way into a conversation in Mexico: people love to recommend dishes and places, and will ask whether you can handle spice. In the central highlands the rainy season runs roughly from late May to October, with sunny mornings and heavy afternoon downpours; the rest of the year is dry, with cool mornings and warm afternoons. Weather is safe small talk with anyone, at a bus stop or in a queue.
recycles: a1-10: en la mañana / en la tarde
units.evidence: The learner says what they like and love with me gusta / me gustan / me encanta, agrees or disagrees with a mí también / tampoco / sí / no, makes a weather comment with hace … or va a llover plus ¿verdad?, and praises food with ¡qué rico!.
sources: ELE L9 (gustar / encantar; también / tampoco / sí / no), L10 (weather; muy vs mucho)
EeM U5 (gustar / encantar, degrees of liking), U8 (weather now)
PCIC Gram. A1 (gustar with the article: me gusta la paella); Tác. C1–C2 ([México] ¿a poco?; moved down, D16)
7K ch.2 (rainy season)
PCIC Saberes 1.3 (seasons), rewritten for Mexico; WP §6.4 (temporada de lluvias / de secas, aguacero)

units.title: Feeling unwell, the pharmacy, emergencies
units.can_do: Say what hurts and how you feel, ask a pharmacist for something, understand dosage, and get help in an emergency.
situations: a pharmacy with a doctor's office next door
a stomach upset in the first weeks

frames.es: Me siento mal.
frames.en: I don't feel well.

frames.es: Me duele la cabeza. / Me duele el estómago.
frames.en: I have a headache. / My stomach hurts.

frames.es: Tengo gripa y un poco de calentura.
frames.en: I have a cold and a bit of a fever.
frames.note: Gripa is the Mexican word for a cold or flu; calentura or fiebre for fever.

frames.es: ¿Tiene algo para la tos? ¿Necesito receta?
frames.en: Do you have something for a cough? Do I need a prescription?

frames.es: Tómese una pastilla cada ocho horas.
frames.en: Take one tablet every eight hours.

frames.es: Me cayó mal la comida.
frames.en: Something I ate disagreed with me.

frames.es: ¡Ayuda! ¡Llamen al 911!
frames.en: Help! Call 911!

frames.es: Está sonando la alerta sísmica: hay que salir.
frames.en: The earthquake alert is sounding: we have to get out.

model_exchanges.situation: At the pharmacy

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.es: Buenas tardes, ¿qué le damos?
lines.en: Good afternoon, what can I get you?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Buenas tardes. Tengo gripa y tos. ¿Tiene algo para la tos?
lines.en: Good afternoon. I have a cold and a cough. Do you have something for the cough?

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.es: Sí, este jarabe. ¿Tiene calentura?
lines.en: Yes, this syrup. Do you have a fever?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Un poco. ¿Necesito receta?
lines.en: A little. Do I need a prescription?

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.es: No, para esto no. Para la calentura, tómese una pastilla cada ocho horas.
lines.en: No, not for this. For the fever, take one tablet every eight hours.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Cada ocho horas?
lines.en: Every eight hours?

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.es: Sí. Y si sigue mal, aquí al lado está el consultorio.
lines.en: Yes. And if you're still unwell, the doctor's office is right next door.

model_exchanges.situation: A stomach upset, with a friend (tú)

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: ¿Qué te pasa? ¿Estás bien?
lines.en: What's wrong? Are you OK?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: No, me siento mal. Me duele el estómago.
lines.en: No, I don't feel well. My stomach hurts.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: Ay, pobre. ¿Qué comiste?
lines.en: Oh, poor you. What did you eat?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Unos tacos en la calle. Creo que me cayó mal la comida.
lines.en: Some tacos on the street. I think something I ate disagreed with me.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.es: Toma mucha agua y ve al consultorio de la farmacia.
lines.en: Drink lots of water and go to the doctor's office at the pharmacy.

model_exchanges.situation: The earthquake alert sounds

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: ¡Está sonando la alerta sísmica! ¡Hay que salir!
lines.en: The earthquake alert is sounding! We have to get out!

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Por dónde?
lines.en: Which way?

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: Por la escalera, no por el elevador. No corra.
lines.en: By the stairs, not the lift. Don't run.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Ya voy!
lines.en: Coming!

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.es: Aquí afuera, lejos de los cables.
lines.en: Out here, away from the cables.

grammar.explain: Me duele + one body part, me duelen + several, always with el / la / los, never mi.
grammar.trap: English says 'my head hurts', but Spanish says 'the head hurts me': me duele la cabeza, not 'me duele mi cabeza' or 'mi cabeza duele'.

grammar.explain: Many conditions are tener + a noun: tengo gripa, tengo tos, tengo calentura.

examples.en: I have a cold / the flu.
I have a bit of a fever.

grammar.trap: Use tener, not estar, with these nouns: 'estoy gripa' is wrong. With an adjective it's estar: estoy enfermo / enferma.

grammar.explain: Me siento + bien, mal or mejor says how you feel.
grammar.trap: Keep the me, and use mal (an adverb), not malo: me siento mal.

grammar.explain: Pharmacists, doctors and emergency staff give instructions with usted commands: tómese, llame, salga.

examples.es: Tómese una pastilla cada ocho horas.
examples.en: Take one tablet every eight hours.

grammar.trap: Cada ocho horas means every eight hours, not eight times a day; repeat the dose back to check.

grammar.point: me cayó mal and hay que as chunks
grammar.explain: Me cayó mal (la comida) is a fixed past for food that disagreed with you; hay que + verb says what has to be done.

examples.en: Something I ate disagreed with me.

grammar.trap: Of a person, me cae mal means 'I don't like him / her', a different meaning. Hay que never changes and doesn't say who: it's a general 'you have to'.

vocabulary.en: doctor's office (often next to a pharmacy)
you have to, we have to

pronunciation: Stress the written accents: es-TÓ-ma-go, SÍS-mi-ca; pastilla and receta follow the rule: pas-TI-lla ('pas-TI-ya'), re-CE-ta ('re-SE-ta').
G before a, o or u is hard, as in 'go': garganta, gripa. G before e or i, and j, sound like a breathy h: urgencias, jarabe.

common_errors.why: Body parts take el / la with doler.
Doler works like gustar: the body part is the subject, me says who.
Several body parts take duelen.
After sentirse, use the adverb mal.
Conditions named by a noun take tener.

units.culture: Many pharmacies have a doctor's office (consultorio) next door or inside, where a short consultation is cheap and quick; it's the usual first stop for a cold or a stomach upset. Pharmacists often advise directly, but antibiotics need a doctor's prescription. The emergency number is 911. In Mexico City and other cities in earthquake zones, the alerta sísmica sounds from street loudspeakers (and on many phones) seconds before a strong quake; there are national drills, and the rule is 'no corro, no grito, no empujo': walk out calmly, use the stairs, and keep away from windows, cables and walls.
units.evidence: The learner says how they feel with me siento mal, says what hurts with me duele(n) + el / la, names a condition with tengo gripa / tos / calentura, asks a pharmacist ¿tiene algo para …? and ¿necesito receta?, checks a dosage by repeating it, and knows to call 911 and follow instructions when the earthquake alert sounds.
sources: EeM U10 (body, doler, remedies; A2, moved to A1 per D22), U16 (doctor's visit, usted commands for dosage)
PCIC Func. A1 3.30 (me duele, tengo fiebre); Gram. A2 (inalienable possession: *me duele mi cabeza); NE A2 13 (health, adapted: gripa, me cayó mal la comida, farmacia con consultorio)
PCIC Saberes 1.12, 1.10 (pharmacy doctors' offices; antibiotics need a prescription; alerta sísmica, simulacros, 911), rewritten for Mexico
WP §6.8 (gripa, calentura, receta, urgencias, cada ocho horas, sismo, alerta sísmica)

units.title: Your first past: what you did today and yesterday
units.can_do: Say what you did today and yesterday, ask whether someone has already done something, and ask how something went.
functions: ask whether something has happened yet
situations: a neighbour asks about your day
a friend checks you got home

frames.es: ¿Ya comiste? — Sí, ya comí. / Todavía no.
frames.en: Have you eaten yet? — Yes, I have. / Not yet.
frames.note: With usted: ¿Ya comió?

frames.es: ¿Qué hiciste ayer?
frames.en: What did you do yesterday?
frames.note: With usted: ¿Qué hizo?

frames.es: Fui al mercado y comí en una fonda.
frames.en: I went to the market and ate at a little restaurant.

frames.es: Ayer estuve en casa todo el día.
frames.en: Yesterday I was at home all day.

frames.es: Hoy me levanté temprano.
frames.en: I got up early today.

frames.es: ¿Cómo te fue? — Me fue muy bien.
frames.en: How did it go? — It went really well.
frames.note: With usted: ¿Cómo le fue?

frames.es: Se me olvidó la cartera.
frames.en: I forgot my wallet.
frames.note: Se me olvidaron for several things: se me olvidaron las llaves.

frames.es: ¿Ya llegaste? — Sí, ya llegué.
frames.en: Are you home yet? — Yes, I'm home.
frames.note: Friends check you got home safely.
