grammar.point: The preterite: regular forms for yo, tú, usted
grammar.explain: For a finished action, -ar verbs end in -é, -aste, -ó, and -er / -ir verbs in -í, -iste, -ió.

examples.en: I bought fruit. / Did you buy fruit? (tú / usted)
I ate at a little restaurant.

grammar.trap: The accent decides the tense: hablo (I speak) vs habló (he, she or usted spoke). Say the last syllable strongly in the preterite.

grammar.point: Three irregular verbs first: fui, hice, estuve
grammar.explain: Ir and ser share one form, fui; hacer becomes hice, hiciste, hizo; estar becomes estuve, estuviste, estuvo.

examples.es: Estuve en casa todo el día.
examples.en: I was at home all day.

grammar.trap: Irregular preterites have no written accent: hice, fui, estuve, not 'hicé'. Fui is both 'I went' and 'I was'; context tells.

grammar.point: ya / todavía no with the preterite
grammar.explain: Mexicans use the preterite for today and for 'already' or 'yet': ¿ya comiste?, sí, ya comí.
grammar.trap: English 'have you eaten?' tempts '¿has comido?', which sounds like Spain; in Mexico it's ¿ya comiste?.

grammar.point: se me olvidó and me fue bien as chunks
grammar.explain: Se me olvidó (it slipped my mind) is how Mexicans say they forgot something; ¿cómo te fue? / me fue bien ask and say how something went.

examples.en: How did it go? — It went well.

grammar.trap: The thing forgotten decides olvidó or olvidaron. 'Olvidé mi cartera' is understood, but se me olvidó is what you'll hear.

grammar.point: Reflexive verbs keep their me in the past
grammar.explain: Verbs like levantarse and bañarse keep me before the verb: me levanté, me bañé.

examples.en: What time did you get up?

grammar.trap: Without the me, levanté means 'I lifted (something)'. Bañarse is the everyday Mexican word for having a shower.

vocabulary.en: to eat; to have the main afternoon meal

vocabulary.form: se me olvidó, se me olvidaron

vocabulary.en: small family restaurant serving home-style food

pronunciation: Stress tells the tense: HA-blo (I speak) vs ha-BLÓ (he / she / usted spoke), LLE-go (I arrive) vs lle-GÓ (arrived), COM-pro vs com-PRÓ. Hit the last syllable firmly in the preterite.
In llegué the u is silent: gue sounds like 'ge' in 'get', so lle-GUÉ ('ye-GE'). The same goes for guitarra and guerra.

common_errors.why: Mexicans use the preterite for today and 'already'.
Each person has its own ending: comí (I), comió (he, she, usted).
Irregular preterites have no accent.
Reflexive verbs keep me.
Plural things take olvidaron.

units.culture: ¿Ya comiste? is everyday small talk in Mexico, and it can also be an invitation to eat; the main meal, la comida, is eaten around 2 to 4 p.m. Asking ¿cómo te fue? about someone's day, trip or appointment is a normal sign of care, and friends often message ¿ya llegaste? after a night out to check you got home safely (avísame cuando llegues = let me know when you get home).
recycles: a1-10: hoy, en la mañana, temprano, tarde
a1-02: no entendí (now a regular preterite)
units.evidence: Asked about their day, the learner answers in the preterite (fui, comí, compré, estuve, hice), uses ya and todavía no with the preterite (¿ya comiste?, todavía no), asks ¿cómo te fue? / ¿qué hiciste? back, and says se me olvidó when they forget something.
sources: ELE Lección opcional (preterite: regular, hacer, venir, ir / ser, estar; '¿Qué hiciste ayer?'; Mexican note on the preterite for today)
EeM U8 (preterite regular and ir / ser / estar; stress hablo / habló); U13 reference (the perfect for today is Peninsular)
PCIC Gram. A2 9.1 (pretérito); Gram. C1 ([Hispanoamérica] preterite where Spain uses the perfect; moved to A1 per D6, D7)
PCIC Func. B1 / Tác. (me olvidé de → se me olvidó; moved down per D15); 7K and PCIC Tác. re-levelling (¿cómo te fue?)

units.title: Family and describing people
units.can_do: Talk about your family and other people's, and describe what people look like and what they're like.
situations: a neighbour shows you family photos
small talk about family, the first topic Mexicans raise

frames.es: Tengo dos hermanos y una hermana.
frames.en: I have two brothers and a sister.
frames.note: hermanos alone can mean siblings: ¿Tiene hermanos? = Do you have brothers and sisters?

frames.es: ¿Tiene hijos? — Sí, una hija y un hijo.
frames.en: Do you have children? — Yes, a daughter and a son.
frames.note: To a friend: ¿Tienes hijos? If they're adults: Ya son grandes.

frames.es: ¿Cómo está su familia?
frames.en: How's your family?
frames.note: A normal opener before any business; answer briefly (Bien, gracias, todos bien) and ask back: ¿Y la suya?

frames.es: Mis papás viven lejos, en mi país.
frames.en: My parents live far away, in my country.
frames.note: papás = parents; adults say mi mamá and mi papá.

frames.es: Es alta, morena y tiene el pelo chino.
frames.en: She's tall, dark and has curly hair.
frames.note: chino = curly, lacio = straight. moreno/a can describe dark hair or darker skin.

frames.es: Es güero y usa lentes.
frames.en: He's fair and wears glasses.
frames.note: güero = fair-haired or light-skinned; vendors also call customers güero or güera, and it's friendly.

frames.es: Es muy buena onda.
frames.en: He's really nice / easy-going.
frames.note: Informal. About someone older or in a formal setting: Es muy amable.

frames.es: Se parece mucho a su mamá.
frames.en: She looks a lot like her mother.

frames.es: Ven, mija, saluda a la señora.
frames.en: Come here, sweetie, say hello to the lady.
frames.note: mija / mijo (from mi hija / mi hijo) is affectionate, also used to adults who aren't family.

model_exchanges.situation: A neighbour shows family photos on her phone

lines.speaker: vecina

lines.en: Look, this is my family.

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.en: He looks a lot like you.

lines.es: ¿Verdad? Y esta es mi nieta. Es bien chistosa.
lines.en: Doesn't he? And this is my granddaughter. She's really funny.

lines.speaker: vecina
lines.es: ¿Y usted tiene hijos?
lines.en: And do you have children?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, dos. Ya son grandes.
lines.en: Yes, two. They're grown up now.

grammar.explain: A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not the owner, and su can mean his, her, their or your (usted).

examples.es: la casa de él, la casa de ella

grammar.trap: English 'his/her' follows the owner; su doesn't, so add de él / de ella when it's unclear. No article before it: mi hermano, not el mi hermano.

grammar.point: ser for what someone is like, tener for features, usar for glasses
grammar.explain: Ser gives what a person is (tall, nice), tener gives features (hair, eyes) and usar or traer what they wear.

examples.es: Usa lentes. / Trae una chamarra roja.
examples.en: He wears glasses. / She's wearing a red jacket.

grammar.trap: What someone is like is ser (es alta, es delgado); estar with build means a change (está muy delgado = he's got thin). Features usually take the article: tiene el pelo chino, tiene los ojos cafés.

grammar.explain: Adjectives in -o change to -a for a woman and add -s for more than one; adjectives in -e or a consonant only add -s / -es.

examples.es: Mi hermano es alto. / Mi hermana es alta.
examples.en: My brother is tall. / My sister is tall.

grammar.trap: Agreement follows the person described, not the speaker: a man describing his sister says es alta.

grammar.explain: In Mexico adults say mi mamá and mi papá, and mis papás means my parents.

examples.es: Voy a ver a mi mamá.
examples.en: I'm going to see my mum.

grammar.trap: Parientes means relatives, not parents; and ¡qué padre! means 'how cool', so padre on its own is less used for 'father' in casual talk.

pronunciation: The d between vowels is soft, the tongue barely touching the teeth: to-ðos, na-ða, cu-ña-ðo. Don't stop the air as in English 'dad'.
In güero the two dots mean you say the u: GWE-ro, not GE-ro. Same in pingüino, vergüenza.

common_errors.why: The adjective agrees with the person described.
For what someone is like, use ser; está alta means 'she's got tall', said of a child who has grown.

common_errors.wrong: Mis parientes viven en mi país. (meaning 'my parents')
common_errors.right: Mis papás viven en mi país.
common_errors.why: Parientes means relatives in general.
Features take tener, not ser.

units.culture: Family is the first topic of small talk: neighbours, vendors and taxi drivers will ask whether you're married, whether you have children and how they are. It's friendly interest, not prying; answer briefly and ask back (¿Y usted?). Adults say mi mamá and mi papá, and many people live with their parents until they marry.
recycles: a1-12: tener for features (tiene dos recámaras)
units.evidence: In a conversation about family, the learner says who's in their family with the right possessives (mi hermana, mis papás), describes one person with es + an agreeing adjective, tiene + a feature and usa lentes, and asks back about the other person's family with usted (¿Y su familia?).
sources: ELE L5 (family, description: es / tiene / lleva, possessives)
EeM U2, U7 (describe people), U12 (extended family)
PCIC Gram. A1 (possessives); NE A1 (description, adapted: güero / moreno, lacio / chino, lentes, ojos cafés; buena onda)
7K (family small talk)

units.title: Becoming a regular: routines and moving to tú
units.can_do: Describe your day and how often you do things, answer "have you settled in?", and accept or ask to switch to tú.
situations: the stall where they know your order
a neighbour asks how you're settling in

frames.es: ¿Lo de siempre?
frames.en: The usual?
frames.note: What a vendor or waiter asks once they know you. Answer: Sí, lo de siempre, por favor.

frames.es: Me levanto a las siete y me baño en la mañana.
frames.en: I get up at seven and shower in the morning.
frames.note: bañarse is the everyday word for 'to shower' in Mexico.

frames.es: Normalmente como a las tres.
frames.en: I usually have lunch at three.
frames.note: comer = to have the comida, the main meal, between about 2 and 4.

frames.es: Voy seguido al mercado.
frames.en: I go to the market often.
frames.note: seguido = often (Mexico); muy seguido = very often.

frames.es: Los domingos salgo a caminar.
frames.en: On Sundays I go out for a walk.
frames.note: los domingos = on Sundays (every Sunday).

frames.es: ¿Ya se acostumbró a vivir aquí?
frames.en: Have you got used to living here yet?
frames.note: To a friend: ¿Ya te acostumbraste?

frames.es: Poco a poco me voy acostumbrando.
frames.en: Little by little I'm getting used to it.

frames.es: Háblame de tú, ¿sí?
frames.en: Use tú with me, OK?
frames.note: An offer to switch to tú. Accept (¡Claro!) and keep using tú with that person.

frames.es: ¿Le puedo hablar de tú?
frames.en: May I use tú with you?
frames.note: Ask people your age or younger, or someone who already uses tú with you; with older people, wait to be offered.

model_exchanges.situation: At the juice stand where they know your order

lines.speaker: señora del puesto
lines.es: ¡Buenos días! ¿Lo de siempre?
lines.en: Good morning! The usual?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, lo de siempre, por favor. Un jugo de naranja.
lines.en: Yes, the usual, please. An orange juice.

lines.speaker: señora del puesto
lines.es: ¿Grande?
lines.en: Large?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, grande. Usted ya me conoce.
lines.en: Yes, large. You know me by now.

lines.speaker: señora del puesto
lines.es: Claro, viene seguido. ¿Ya se acostumbró a vivir aquí?
lines.en: Of course, you come often. Have you got used to living here yet?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Poco a poco me voy acostumbrando. Me encanta el mercado.
lines.en: Little by little I'm getting used to it. I love the market.

lines.speaker: señora del puesto
lines.es: ¡Qué bueno! Aquí está su jugo.
lines.en: Great! Here's your juice.

lines.speaker: vecino

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: ¡Ah, ya se acostumbró!
lines.en: Ah, you've got used to it!

lines.en: Sure! Then you too, OK?

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.speaker: vecina

lines.en: Very well, thanks.

grammar.point: Reflexive verbs: levantarse, bañarse, acostarse, acostumbrarse
grammar.explain: These verbs carry a pronoun that matches the subject (me, te, se, nos, se), placed before the conjugated verb.

examples.en: What time do you go to bed?

grammar.trap: English 'I get up' has no 'myself', so learners drop the pronoun; levanto a las siete means 'I lift at seven'. Say me levanto.

grammar.point: Stem changes and yo forms in -go
grammar.explain: Some verbs change their stem vowel when it is stressed (e > ie, o > ue, e > i), and a few add -g- in the yo form only.

examples.en: I go to bed, I start, I ask for
I go out, do, put, have, come
we go to bed, we start (no change)

grammar.trap: The change doesn't happen with nosotros: nos acostamos, not nos acuestamos.

grammar.point: How often: siempre, seguido, a veces, casi nunca
grammar.explain: Frequency words go before the verb or at the end; nunca before the verb needs no other no.

examples.en: I always have breakfast at home.
I often go to the market.

examples.es: Casi nunca ceno. / No ceno casi nunca.
Voy una vez a la semana.

grammar.trap: For 'often', Mexicans say seguido; a menudo is understood but sounds bookish.

grammar.explain: Ir + a verb in -ando or -iendo shows something happening little by little; learn it as a chunk for now.

examples.es: Poco a poco me voy acostumbrando.
examples.en: Little by little I'm getting used to it.

grammar.trap: Me voy acostumbrando (I'm getting used to it) is not ya estoy acostumbrado (I'm used to it now).

grammar.explain: Keep usted with older people and anyone you don't know well; switch when the other person offers, or after asking.

examples.en: May I use tú with you?

grammar.trap: Using tú too soon is the commoner mistake in Mexico. Once you've switched with someone, don't go back to usted: it sounds cold.

vocabulary.en: to eat; to have the main midday meal

pronunciation: The changed vowel is the stressed one: me a-CUES-to, em-PIE-zo, but nos a-cos-TA-mos, em-pe-ZA-mos.
The pronoun runs into the verb with no break: me levanto sounds like one word, me-le-VAN-to.

common_errors.why: Reflexive verbs need their pronoun.
salir has -g- in the yo form.
No stem change with nosotros.

common_errors.wrong: Almuerzo a las tres. (meaning the main meal)
common_errors.why: In much of Mexico almuerzo is a mid-morning meal; the main meal is la comida.
Going back to usted after agreeing to tú sounds distant.

units.culture: Becoming a regular matters: stallholders and waiters remember your order (¿lo de siempre?), may add a little extra (un pilón) and ask after your family. The comida, the main meal, is eaten between about 2 and 4 pm and dinner is light. With older people, wait for them to offer tú; among younger people and colleagues tú comes quickly.
recycles: a1-10: a las siete, en la mañana
units.evidence: Asked about their day, the learner gives three or four steps of their routine with reflexive verbs and at least one -go or stem-changing verb, says how often with seguido or casi nunca, answers ¿Ya se acostumbró?, and, when offered tú, accepts and keeps using tú with that person.
sources: ELE L11 (routine, stem changes, reflexives), L12 (frequency)
EeM U3 (reflexive routine)
PCIC Gram. A2 (irregular presents); NE A1 (meals, adapted: comida 2–4); NG C1 (voy acostumbrándome: moved down)
PCIC Saberes (meal times; regular customer, ¿lo de siempre?)
7K (switching to tú: háblame de tú)
WP (seguido)

units.title: Eating out
units.can_do: Order a set lunch or a meal, ask what's in a dish, mention an allergy, ask for and split the bill, tip, and compliment the food.
situations: a set lunch at a fonda
telling the cook it was good

frames.es: ¿Qué trae la comida corrida?
frames.en: What comes with the set lunch?
frames.note: comida corrida = the set lunch at a fonda or cocina económica: soup, rice or pasta, a main, a drink and often dessert.

frames.es: Hay sopa de fideo, arroz y, de guisado, tinga o milanesa.
frames.en: There's noodle soup, rice and, for the main, tinga or breaded steak.
frames.note: guisado = the main dish of a set lunch.

frames.es: ¿Lleva cacahuate?
frames.en: Does it have peanuts in it?
frames.note: ¿Qué lleva? = What's in it?

frames.es: Soy alérgico a los mariscos.
frames.en: I'm allergic to seafood.
frames.note: A woman says alérgica.

frames.es: Joven, ¿me trae la cuenta, por favor?
frames.en: Excuse me, could you bring the bill, please?
frames.note: joven or señorita is how you call the waiter; a signing gesture in the air also works.

frames.es: ¿Junto o separado?
frames.en: Together or separate?
frames.note: Whether to put everyone on one bill.

frames.es: ¿Va a querer factura?
frames.en: Will you need a tax invoice?
frames.note: A factura is an official invoice for tax purposes; most people answer No, gracias.

frames.es: ¿Me trae la terminal, por favor?
frames.en: Could you bring the card machine, please?
frames.note: The waiter brings the terminal to the table.

frames.es: ¡Estuvo riquísimo!
frames.en: That was delicious!
frames.note: estuvo for a meal you've just finished; while eating: ¡Está riquísimo!

model_exchanges.situation: A set lunch at a fonda

lines.en: Yes. What's on today?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿La tinga pica?
lines.en: Is the tinga spicy?

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: Poquito nada más.
lines.en: Just a little.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Entonces sopa de fideo y tinga, por favor.
lines.en: Then noodle soup and tinga, please.

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: ¿Y de tomar? Hoy es de jamaica.
lines.en: And to drink? Today it's hibiscus.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, de jamaica, gracias.
lines.en: Yes, hibiscus, thanks.

model_exchanges.situation: Mentioning an allergy in a restaurant

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Disculpe, ¿el mole lleva cacahuate?
lines.en: Excuse me, does the mole have peanuts in it?

lines.speaker: mesero
lines.es: Sí, lleva cacahuate y ajonjolí.
lines.en: Yes, it has peanuts and sesame.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Ay, soy alérgica al cacahuate. ¿Qué me recomienda?
lines.en: Oh, I'm allergic to peanuts. What do you recommend?

lines.speaker: mesero
lines.es: Las enchiladas verdes no llevan. Son de pollo, con crema y queso.
lines.en: The green enchiladas don't have any. They're chicken, with cream and cheese.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Perfecto, unas enchiladas verdes, por favor.
lines.en: Perfect, green enchiladas, please.

model_exchanges.situation: Paying after dinner with a friend

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Joven, ¿nos trae la cuenta, por favor?
lines.en: Excuse me, could you bring us the bill, please?

lines.speaker: mesero
lines.es: Con gusto. ¿Junto o separado?
lines.en: Of course. Together or separate?

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Junto, y me la da a mí. Yo invito.
lines.en: Together, and give it to me. It's on me.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Muchas gracias! La próxima invito yo.
lines.en: Thanks so much! Next time it's on me.

lines.speaker: mesero
lines.es: ¿Va a querer factura?
lines.en: Will you need a tax invoice?

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: No, gracias. ¿Me trae la terminal?
lines.en: No, thanks. Could you bring the card machine?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Estuvo riquísimo todo!
lines.en: Everything was delicious!

grammar.point: llevar and traer for what's in a dish or a meal
grammar.explain: To ask what a dish contains, use llevar; to ask what a set meal includes, use traer.

examples.en: Does it have onion in it?
What comes with the set lunch?

grammar.trap: The dish is the subject, so the verb stays singular even before a plural: ¿El mole lleva chiles? Tener is also heard, but ¿lleva…? is what waiters expect.

grammar.explain: A present-tense question with me or nos is the polite way to ask staff for something.

examples.en: Could you bring me another tortilla, please?
Could you bring us the bill?
Could you bring me the menu?

grammar.trap: A bare command (tráigame la cuenta) sounds bossy unless softened; the question form is the safe default.

grammar.point: estar for how food tastes; estuvo for a meal just finished
grammar.explain: Estar describes how this food tastes now; estuvo sums up a meal you've just had.
grammar.trap: Es rico describes a dish in general (or means a person is rich); for the plate in front of you, use está.

grammar.explain: Add -ísimo to an adjective, dropping the final vowel, to mean 'really' or 'extremely'.
grammar.trap: Spelling keeps the sound: rico > riquísimo. Never add muy: muy riquísimo is wrong.

vocabulary.en: main dish, stew (of a set lunch)

pronunciation: b, d and g between vowels are soft: la sopa de fideo (de fi-ðe-o), el guisado (gi-SA-ðo), agua (A-ɣwa). Let the air through instead of stopping it.
-ísimo always takes the stress on the í: ri-QUÍ-si-mo, bue-NÍ-si-mo, ca-RÍ-si-mo.

common_errors.why: For the food you're eating now, use estar.
-ísimo already means 'very'.
Alérgico takes a.
Asking for the bill uses traer, as a polite question.

units.culture: At a table, tip 10–15%: the waiter brings the card terminal to you, so say how much to add (con el diez por ciento, por favor) or leave cash. A fonda's comida corrida is a cheap set lunch served from early afternoon; the bill never comes until you ask, and catching the waiter's eye or miming a signature is fine. Saying ¡provecho! to people eating as you pass their table is normal.
recycles: a1-05: Me da …, por favor / ¿Pica? / ¿Me regala una servilleta?
units.evidence: At a fonda or restaurant the learner asks what the set lunch includes or what a dish has (¿qué trae?, ¿lleva…?), mentions an allergy with soy alérgico/a a + article, asks for the bill with ¿me trae / nos trae…?, answers ¿junto o separado?, and thanks with ¡Estuvo riquísimo!
sources: EeM U5 (set menu), U15 (bar and bill: ¿me cobra?)
PCIC Func. A2 (¿me trae …?); NE A1 (comida corrida, mesero, joven, la cuenta)
PCIC Saberes (comida corrida; tips 10–15%; card terminal to the table)
WP (platillo, factura, propina)
7K (praise the food)

units.title: Shopping for clothes, exchanges and returns
units.can_do: Browse, try things on, ask for another size, compare, buy, and exchange or return something.

frames.es: Nomás estoy viendo, gracias.
frames.en: I'm just looking, thanks.

frames.es: ¿Me la puedo probar?
frames.en: Can I try it on?
frames.note: la for a feminine item (la chamarra, la playera); lo for a masculine one (el suéter): ¿Me lo puedo probar? Also heard: ¿Me lo puedo medir?

frames.es: ¿Qué talla busca?
frames.en: What size are you looking for?
frames.note: Clothes go by chica, mediana, grande (CH, M, G).

frames.es: ¿Qué número calza?
frames.en: What shoe size are you?
frames.note: Mexican shoe sizes roughly follow foot length in centimetres: Calzo del 26.

frames.es: Me queda grande. ¿Tiene una más chica?
frames.en: It's too big for me. Do you have a smaller one?
frames.note: me queda chico / grande / bien / apretado = it's small / big / fine / tight on me.

frames.es: Esta chamarra es más cara que la otra.
frames.en: This jacket is more expensive than the other one.

frames.es: Me la llevo.
frames.en: I'll take it.
frames.note: Me lo llevo for a masculine item; me los llevo for several (los tenis).

frames.es: ¿Lo puedo cambiar? Aquí está el ticket.
frames.en: Can I exchange it? Here's the receipt.
frames.note: ticket = till receipt.

frames.es: Solo hay cambios con ticket.
frames.en: Exchanges only with a receipt.
frames.note: Many shops exchange but don't refund: No hay devoluciones.

model_exchanges.situation: Trying something on in a department store

lines.speaker: vendedora
lines.es: ¿Le puedo ayudar en algo?
lines.en: Can I help you with anything?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Nomás estoy viendo, gracias. Bueno… ¿tiene esta playera en azul?
lines.en: Just looking, thanks. Well… do you have this T-shirt in blue?

lines.speaker: vendedora
lines.es: Sí. ¿Qué talla busca?
lines.en: Yes. What size are you looking for?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Mediana. ¿Me la puedo probar?
lines.en: Medium. Can I try it on?

lines.speaker: vendedora
lines.es: Claro, los probadores están al fondo.
lines.en: Of course, the fitting rooms are at the back.

lines.speaker: vendedora
lines.es: ¿Cómo le quedó?
lines.en: How did it fit?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me queda un poco grande. ¿Tiene una más chica?
lines.en: It's a bit big on me. Do you have a smaller one?

lines.speaker: vendedora
lines.es: Sí, aquí está la chica.
lines.en: Yes, here's the small.

model_exchanges.situation: Buying trainers at a market stall

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Cuánto cuestan estos tenis?
lines.en: How much are these trainers?

lines.speaker: vendedor
lines.es: Ochocientos. ¿Qué número calza?
lines.en: Eight hundred. What size are you?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Del veintisiete.
lines.en: Twenty-seven.

lines.speaker: vendedor
lines.es: Aquí tiene. Pruébeselos.
lines.en: Here you are. Try them on.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me quedan bien. Pero son más caros que los negros, ¿no?
lines.en: They fit well. But they're more expensive than the black ones, aren't they?

lines.speaker: vendedor
lines.es: Sí, pero son mejores. Duran más.
lines.en: Yes, but they're better. They last longer.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Bueno, me los llevo.
lines.en: OK, I'll take them.

model_exchanges.situation: Taking something back

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Buenas tardes. Compré esta chamarra ayer, pero me queda chica. ¿La puedo cambiar?
lines.en: Good afternoon. I bought this jacket yesterday, but it's small on me. Can I exchange it?

lines.speaker: cajera
lines.es: ¿Trae su ticket?
lines.en: Do you have your receipt?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, aquí está.
lines.en: Yes, here it is.

lines.speaker: cajera
lines.es: Muy bien. Solo hay cambios, no devoluciones. ¿La quiere en otra talla?
lines.en: Fine. We only do exchanges, not refunds. Do you want it in another size?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí, en grande, por favor.
lines.en: Yes, in large, please.

grammar.point: Direct object pronouns: lo, la, los, las
grammar.explain: To avoid repeating a thing or person, use lo, la, los or las to match it, before the conjugated verb or joined to the end of an infinitive.

examples.en: The trainers? I'll try them on.

grammar.trap: The pronoun matches the thing, not you: a man buying a shirt says me la llevo. Mexico uses lo / la, not le, for things and people (lo compré, la conozco).

grammar.explain: Quedar works like gustar: the clothes are the subject and me, te or le says who they fit.

examples.es: Te quedan muy bien esos jeans.
examples.en: Those jeans look great on you.

grammar.trap: Plural clothes take quedan: los pantalones me quedan chicos.

grammar.explain: Más or menos + adjective + que compares two things; mejor and peor replace más bueno and más malo.

examples.es: Esta es más cara que la otra.
examples.en: This one is more expensive than the other one.

grammar.trap: 'Than' is que, not como: más cara que la otra.

grammar.explain: Colours in -o change for gender and number; colours in -e or a consonant only add -s or -es.

examples.es: una playera roja, unos tenis rojos
una chamarra azul, unos jeans azules

grammar.trap: Brown is café in Mexico (ojos cafés, zapatos cafés); marrón sounds Spanish.

grammar.explain: Probarse means to try on; the reflexive pronoun comes first, then lo / la.

examples.es: Me los probé y me quedan bien.
examples.en: I tried them on and they fit.

grammar.trap: The order never flips: me la, not la me.

pronunciation: Adding pronouns never moves the stress, so a written accent appears: PRUE-be-se-los, pro-BÁR-me-la.
r between vowels is one quick tap, rr is rolled: caro (expensive) vs carro (car).

common_errors.wrong: (about a shirt, la camisa) Me lo llevo.
common_errors.why: The pronoun matches the item's gender.

common_errors.wrong: Es más cara como la otra.
common_errors.right: Es más cara que la otra.
common_errors.why: Comparatives with más take que.
One item, singular verb.
Mexico uses lo / la for things.

units.culture: Clothes come in CH, M and G (chica, mediana, grande) and shoes in Mexican sizes, roughly centimetres (Calzo del 26). Many shops exchange with the ticket but don't refund, so ask before paying (¿Hay devoluciones?). Prices in shops are fixed; at a market or tianguis clothing stall a polite ¿Me lo deja en…? may get a small discount.
units.evidence: In a shop the learner turns away help with nomás estoy viendo, asks to try something on with the right pronoun (¿me la puedo probar?), says how it fits with me queda / me quedan, compares two items with más … que, and asks to exchange something with its ticket.
sources: EeM U9 (clothes, lo / la / los / las, comparatives, colours)
ELE L6 (me lo llevo)
PCIC Gram. A2 (clitics); Gén. A2 sample (shop dialogue: ¿puedo probármelo?, ¿cómo le queda?)
PCIC NE B1–B2 (cambio / devolución, barata)
WP (chamarra, playera, talla / número, me queda grande, ticket)

units.title: Tell what you did
units.can_do: Tell someone what you did at the weekend or on a trip, with the common irregular verbs.
situations: telling a friend about a trip

frames.es: ¿Qué tal tu fin de semana?
frames.en: How was your weekend?
frames.note: Also: ¿Qué hiciste el fin? To usted: ¿Qué tal su fin de semana?

frames.es: Fuimos a un pueblo cerca de aquí.
frames.en: We went to a little town near here.

frames.es: La pasamos muy bien.
frames.en: We had a really good time.
frames.note: Mexico says pasarla bien; nos la pasamos bien is also common.

frames.es: Estuvo muy bonito, pero llegamos tarde por el tráfico.
frames.en: It was lovely, but we got there late because of the traffic.

frames.es: Conocí a tu vecina.
frames.en: I met your neighbour.
frames.note: conocer in the preterite = to meet someone for the first time.

frames.es: Anoche no pude dormir.
frames.en: I couldn't sleep last night.

frames.es: Antier fui al doctor.
frames.en: I went to the doctor the day before yesterday.
frames.note: antier = the day before yesterday (anteayer is also said).

frames.es: El domingo hice de comer y vinieron unos amigos.
frames.en: On Sunday I cooked and some friends came over.
frames.note: hacer de comer = to cook a meal (Mexico).

model_exchanges.situation: Monday morning small talk with a neighbour

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: ¡Buenos días! ¿Qué tal su fin de semana?
lines.en: Good morning! How was your weekend?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Muy bien, gracias. Fuimos a un pueblo cerca de aquí.
lines.en: Very good, thanks. We went to a little town near here.

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: ¡Qué bien! ¿Y qué hicieron?
lines.en: Great! And what did you do?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Caminamos mucho, comimos en el mercado y subimos al cerro.
lines.en: We walked a lot, ate at the market and climbed the hill.

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: ¿Y cómo regresaron?
lines.en: And how did you get back?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: En camión. Llegamos tarde por el tráfico, pero la pasamos muy bien.
lines.en: By bus. We got back late because of the traffic, but we had a really good time.

model_exchanges.situation: Telling a friend about a bad night

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Te ves cansado. ¿Qué te pasó?
lines.en: You look tired. What happened?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Anoche no pude dormir. Los vecinos hicieron una fiesta hasta las tres.
lines.en: I couldn't sleep last night. The neighbours had a party until three.

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: ¡Híjole! ¿Y no les dijiste nada?
lines.en: Oh no! And you didn't say anything to them?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: No, no quise decir nada. Al final me puse los audífonos.
lines.en: No, I didn't want to say anything. In the end I put my earphones on.

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Ay, pobrecito.
lines.en: Oh, poor thing.

model_exchanges.situation: Catching up about someone you met

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Ayer conocí a tu vecina, la del perro.
lines.en: Yesterday I met your neighbour, the one with the dog.

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: ¿A doña Carmen? ¿Dónde la conociste?
lines.en: Doña Carmen? Where did you meet her?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: En la tienda. Me dijo que es tu tía.
lines.en: At the shop. She told me she's your aunt.

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: Sí, es mi tía. ¿Y qué más te dijo?
lines.en: Yes, she's my aunt. And what else did she tell you?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Nada malo, te lo juro.
lines.en: Nothing bad, I swear.

grammar.explain: A group of everyday verbs takes a new stem and the endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron, with no written accent.

examples.es: tener > tuve, estar > estuve, poder > pude, poner > puse
examples.en: I had, I was, I could, I put

examples.es: hacer > hice (él hizo), venir > vine, querer > quise, saber > supe
examples.en: I did, I came, I tried/wanted, I found out

grammar.trap: No accent on these: tuve, hizo, vino, not tuvé or hizó. Decir drops the i: dijeron, not dijieron.

grammar.explain: Ayer, anoche, antier, el sábado, la semana pasada and hace + time go with the preterite.

examples.en: Last night we had tacos for dinner.

examples.es: Hace dos días llegó mi hermana.
examples.en: My sister arrived two days ago.

examples.es: La semana pasada fui al doctor.
examples.en: Last week I went to the doctor.

grammar.trap: 'Two days ago' is hace dos días, with hace first; don't put 'ago' at the end.

grammar.explain: When the direct object is a specific person, put a before it.

examples.es: Vi a Pedro en el mercado.
examples.en: I saw Pedro at the market.
I saw the new market. (no a for places)

grammar.trap: English has nothing here, and conocí tu vecina sounds wrong to Mexican ears.

grammar.point: Verbs that change meaning in the preterite
grammar.explain: In the preterite, conocer means met for the first time, saber means found out, and no querer means refused.

examples.es: Conocí a mucha gente en la fiesta.
examples.en: I met a lot of people at the party.
I refused to go / I didn't want to go.

grammar.trap: Don't use encontrar for meeting people: encontrar is to find (me encontré con Ana = I bumped into Ana).

grammar.explain: Mexico says pasarla bien for 'to have a good time'; the la doesn't refer to anything.

examples.en: We had a really good time.
How was the party for you?

grammar.trap: Lo pasamos bien is the Spanish form; in Mexico the pronoun is la.

vocabulary.en: to meet (in the preterite); to know

pronunciation: Stress tells the tense: camino (I walk) vs caminó (she walked), llego vs llegó. The irregulars stay stressed on the stem: TU-ve, HI-zo, PU-de.
Words link in fast speech: fuimos a un pueblo sounds like fui-mo-saun-PUE-blo; listen for the a.

common_errors.why: hacer has an irregular preterite: hice, hizo.
Irregular preterites have no written accent.
A specific person as object needs the personal a.
Mexico uses la in this expression.

units.culture: Monday small talk starts with ¿Qué tal el fin? or ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana?, and people expect a short story back, not just bien. Weekend outings to nearby pueblos and markets and long Sunday family meals are typical, and Sunday-evening traffic back into the big cities is the classic excuse for arriving late.
recycles: a1-15: fui, hice, estuve / ¿Cómo te fue?
a2-02: normalmente + present vs ayer + preterite
units.evidence: Asked about the weekend, the learner tells three or four linked events in the preterite, including at least two irregular verbs (fuimos, tuve, hice, pude), says how it went with la pasamos bien or estuvo + adjective, and uses the personal a when naming someone they met.
sources: ELE Opc ("¿saliste? me quedé en casa", conocí = met)
EeM U8, U10 (Barrancas del Cobre blog: "nos la pasamos muy bien"), U11 (biography)
PCIC Gram. A2 (preterite, personal a); NG B1 (anteayer → antier, anoche); NG B2 (pasarla bien [México])

units.title: Plans, invitations and soft refusals
units.can_do: Talk about plans, invite, accept, decline politely with a reason, and recognise a Mexican "no" that sounds like a maybe.
situations: a neighbour invites you to a party

frames.es: ¿Qué vas a hacer el sábado?
frames.en: What are you doing on Saturday?
frames.note: To usted: ¿Qué va a hacer el sábado?

frames.es: ¿Quieres ir por unos tacos el viernes?
frames.en: Do you want to go for tacos on Friday?
frames.note: ir por = to go and get (food, a drink): ir por un café.

frames.es: ¡Va! / ¡Sale! / ¡Órale!
frames.en: Sure! / OK! / You're on!
frames.note: All mean yes; órale is the most enthusiastic. Informal; with older people: ¡Claro!, con mucho gusto.

frames.es: Me encantaría, pero no puedo. Es que tengo que trabajar.
frames.en: I'd love to, but I can't. I have to work.

frames.es: No sé si pueda, pero hago la lucha.
frames.en: I don't know if I can, but I'll try.
frames.note: Polite and warm, but it often means no.

frames.es: A ver si puedo. / Déjame ver. / Ahí vemos.
frames.en: I'll see if I can. / Let me see. / We'll see.
frames.note: Often a soft no. If it matters, ask again nearer the day rather than pressing now.

frames.es: Te invito un café.
frames.en: Let me buy you a coffee.
frames.note: invitar means you're paying.

frames.es: Quedamos de vernos a las seis en la esquina.
frames.en: We agreed to meet at six on the corner.
frames.note: quedar de + infinitive = to agree to do something.

model_exchanges.situation: A neighbour invites you to a family get-together

lines.speaker: vecina
lines.es: Oiga, el sábado vamos a hacer una carne asada por el cumpleaños de mi esposo. ¿Por qué no viene?
lines.en: Listen, on Saturday we're having a barbecue for my husband's birthday. Why don't you come?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Muchas gracias! ¿A qué hora?
lines.en: Thank you so much! What time?

lines.speaker: vecina
lines.es: Como a las cuatro. Nada formal.
lines.en: Around four. Nothing formal.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me encantaría. ¿Llevo algo?
lines.en: I'd love to. Shall I bring something?

lines.speaker: vecina
lines.es: No, nada, nomás venga.
lines.en: No, nothing, just come.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Bueno, llevo un postre. ¡Gracias por la invitación!
lines.en: OK, I'll bring a dessert. Thanks for the invitation!

model_exchanges.situation: Declining a friend and offering another day

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: ¿Quieres ir por unos tacos el viernes?
lines.en: Do you want to go for tacos on Friday?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me encantaría, pero no puedo. Es que tengo que trabajar hasta tarde.
lines.en: I'd love to, but I can't. I have to work late.

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: Ni modo. ¿Y el domingo?
lines.en: Oh well. And Sunday?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Va! El domingo sí puedo.
lines.en: Sure! On Sunday I can.

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: Sale. Quedamos de vernos a las seis en la esquina, ¿no?
lines.en: Deal. So we'll meet at six on the corner, right?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Perfecto. Ahí nos vemos.
lines.en: Perfect. See you there.

model_exchanges.situation: A colleague gives a soft no (hago la lucha and luego te aviso usually mean she won't come)

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Vienes a mi casa el sábado? Voy a cocinar.
lines.en: Will you come to my place on Saturday? I'm going to cook.

lines.speaker: compañera
lines.es: ¡Ay, qué amable! No sé si pueda, pero hago la lucha.
lines.en: Oh, how kind! I don't know if I can, but I'll try.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Entonces te espero?
lines.en: So shall I expect you?

lines.speaker: compañera
lines.es: Déjame ver, ¿sí? Luego te aviso.
lines.en: Let me see, OK? I'll let you know.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sale, me avisas.
lines.en: OK, let me know.

grammar.explain: Ir a + infinitive is the everyday way to talk about plans and the future.

examples.en: What are you doing on Saturday?

examples.es: Voy a ver a unos amigos.
examples.en: I'm going to see some friends.

examples.es: Vamos a hacer una carne asada.

grammar.trap: Don't drop the a: voy a ir, not voy ir. The future in -ré (iré) sounds formal for plans in Mexico.

grammar.explain: Tener que + infinitive says what you have to do, and is the usual reason for saying no.

examples.en: We have to go to the doctor.
Do you have to work on Saturday?

grammar.trap: Keep the que: tengo que ir, never tengo ir.

grammar.point: es que … for a reason or an excuse
grammar.explain: Start a reason with es que…; it softens a refusal or an apology.

examples.en: It's just that I have to work.

examples.es: Es que ya quedé con mi familia.
examples.en: It's just that I've already arranged something with my family.

examples.es: Perdón por llegar tarde, es que el camión tardó mucho.
examples.en: Sorry I'm late, the bus took ages.

grammar.trap: A bare no puedo sounds abrupt; Mexicans almost always give a reason.

grammar.explain: Te invito … means 'it's on me': whoever invites pays.

examples.en: Let me buy you a coffee.

grammar.trap: Don't say te invito unless you mean to pay; to suggest going together, say ¿vamos por un café?

grammar.explain: Quedar de + infinitive means to agree to do something together.

examples.es: Quedamos de vernos a las seis.
examples.en: We agreed to meet at six.

grammar.trap: Quedar de vernos (agree to meet) is not quedarse (to stay).

grammar.explain: A ver si puedo, déjame ver, ahí vemos and hago la lucha often mean no; to decline yourself at this level, use me encantaría, pero … + es que.

examples.es: No sé si pueda, pero hago la lucha.
examples.en: I don't know if I can, but I'll try.
I'd love to, but I can't.

grammar.trap: Don't take a maybe as a yes, and don't press for a firm answer: it puts the other person on the spot.

vocabulary.en: to try, to do your best
oh well, nothing to be done

pronunciation: Plans run together: voy a ir sounds like vo-ya-IR, vamos a ver like va-mo-sa-VER. Listen for the little a.
Tone carries the answer: a short, falling ¡Sale! is a yes; a long, rising A ver… with a pause is usually hesitation.

common_errors.why: ir a + infinitive needs the a.
tener que needs que.

common_errors.wrong: Quedamos a vernos a las seis.
common_errors.right: Quedamos de vernos a las seis.
common_errors.why: In Mexico, quedar takes de + infinitive.

common_errors.right: Me encantaría, pero no puedo. Es que …
common_errors.why: A refusal without thanks and a reason sounds rude.

units.culture: Invitations are generous and some are made out of courtesy (de cumplido); a real one comes with a day and a time. A Mexican 'no' is rarely said straight: a ver si puedo, ahí vemos or hago la lucha usually mean no, and nobody minds if you then don't come. Whoever invites pays, and parties start well after the stated time, though appointments with doctors and offices don't.
recycles: a1-10: ¿Nos vemos el sábado a las cinco? — ¡Sale!
units.evidence: The learner invites someone with ¿quieres ir por …? or te invito …, accepts with va or sale, declines with me encantaría, pero … + es que + a reason, fixes a time with quedamos de vernos, and, when a character answers a ver si puedo or ahí vemos, shows they took it as a probable no (for example by suggesting another day).
sources: EeM U7 (invite / accept / decline, quedar), U10 (ir a)
PCIC Func. A2 (te invito a …; polite refusals); Func. B1 (me encantaría, pero …; es que); Tác. B1 (ir a to put off: no sé si voy a poder)
7K (soft no: hago la lucha, luego lo platicamos, al rato vemos)
PCIC Saberes (indirect no: a ver si puedo, ahí vemos; invitar = paying; invitations made out of courtesy)

units.title: Phone, WhatsApp and appointments
units.can_do: Answer and make short calls, ask for someone, understand the receptionist, make an appointment, and use the usual WhatsApp phrases.
situations: calling a clinic or a business
a call to the wrong number

frames.es: ¿Bueno?
frames.en: Hello? (answering the phone)
frames.note: How Mexicans answer the phone, with a rising tone.

frames.es: ¿Se encuentra la licenciada Ruiz?
frames.en: Is Ms Ruiz there?
frames.note: licenciado / licenciada is the usual title for someone with a degree, especially in offices.

frames.es: ¿De parte de quién?
frames.en: Who's calling?
frames.note: Answer: De parte de … .

frames.es: Permítame tantito. / Ahorita no se encuentra.
frames.en: One moment. / She's not here right now.

frames.es: ¿Le puedo dejar un recado?
frames.en: Can I leave her a message?

frames.es: Creo que se equivocó de número.
frames.en: I think you've got the wrong number.

frames.es: Quisiera hacer una cita para el jueves 15.
frames.en: I'd like to make an appointment for Thursday the 15th.

frames.es: Te mando un audio. / Te marco al rato.
frames.en: I'll send you a voice note. / I'll call you in a bit.
frames.note: marcar = to call (Mexico); un audio = a WhatsApp voice message.

frames.es: Mándame tu ubicación.
frames.en: Send me your location.

lines.speaker: recepcionista

lines.en: In what name?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: A nombre de … . ¿Se lo deletreo?

model_exchanges.situation: Calling for someone who isn't in

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: ¿Bueno?
lines.en: Hello?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Buenas tardes. ¿Se encuentra la licenciada Ruiz?
lines.en: Good afternoon. Is Ms Ruiz there?

lines.speaker: señora
lines.es: ¿De parte de quién?
lines.en: Who's calling?

lines.speaker: newcomer

lines.en: I can see you!

grammar.explain: Quisiera + infinitive or noun is a polite 'I'd like', the right tone on the phone and in offices.

examples.en: I'd like to make an appointment.

examples.es: Quisiera hablar con el licenciado Sánchez.
examples.en: I'd like to speak to Mr Sánchez.

grammar.trap: Quiero is fine for ordering at a counter but sounds blunt in requests like these; learn quisiera as a fixed form.

grammar.point: te and le: 'to you', 'to him / her'
grammar.explain: Te (tú) and le (usted, him, her) say who receives something; they go before the conjugated verb.

examples.en: I'll send you a voice note.
Shall I tell her you called?

grammar.trap: With usted the pronoun is le, the same as for him or her, so ¿le marco mañana? can mean 'shall I call you (usted) tomorrow?'

grammar.explain: Dates use the plain number with el, and the weekday can go first; only the 1st is primero.

examples.es: el 3 de mayo, el primero de junio

grammar.trap: No other ordinals: el 3 de mayo, not el tercero de mayo.

grammar.explain: Small words soften requests and time: tantito (a little), un momentito, ahorita (now, in a moment, soon).

examples.en: She's not here at the moment.

grammar.trap: Ahorita no se encuentra means 'not here right now', but ahorita te marco can mean in a minute or much later.

grammar.explain: People in offices are called by title: licenciado/a, ingeniero/a, doctor/a, often with the surname.

examples.en: Good afternoon (to a woman with a degree).

examples.es: El doctor llega a las cuatro.

grammar.trap: Use the article when talking about someone (el ingeniero Pérez), not when talking to them (Buenas tardes, ingeniero).

pronunciation: ¿Bueno? on the phone rises at the end; a falling bueno means 'well' or 'OK'.
¿Se encuentra? runs together as se-en-CUEN-tra; listen for the whole chunk rather than the separate words.

common_errors.why: You speak con someone, not a.
An appointment is una cita.
Dates use the plain number.

common_errors.right: Te marco más tarde. / Te regreso la llamada.
common_errors.why: 'Call back' isn't built with atrás.

units.culture: Mexicans answer the phone with ¿Bueno? and businesses with their name. WhatsApp is how almost everything gets arranged: voice notes (audios) are normal even when long, and sharing your location is the standard way to meet up. Doctors, salons and many services book appointments by WhatsApp.
recycles: a1-02: ¿Me lo puede repetir? / ¿Cómo se escribe?
a1-10: ahorita, al rato, days of the week
a1-06: phone numbers read in pairs
units.evidence: On a call the learner answers with ¿Bueno?, asks for someone with ¿se encuentra …?, says who's calling with de parte de …, handles ahorita no se encuentra by leaving a message or saying they'll call back, books an appointment with quisiera + a date said as el jueves 15, and uses te mando / te marco when arranging by WhatsApp.
sources: EeM U4 (booking by phone), U7 (phone, leaving a message)
PCIC Func. A2 (phone: ¿de parte de quién?, se equivoca); Gén. A2 (very short phone calls); Tác. A2 (Mexican ¿bueno?)
PCIC Saberes (WhatsApp voice notes)
WP (te marco, ¿bueno?, mándame la ubicación, un audio)
PCIC NG (estamos a 15 → hoy es 15)

units.title: Directions and transport, part two
units.can_do: Give directions as well as follow them, use the metro's lines and transfers, and buy a long-distance bus ticket.

buying a bus ticket at the terminal

frames.es: Luego da vuelta a la izquierda en el semáforo.
frames.en: Then turn left at the traffic lights.
frames.note: To usted: dé vuelta.

grammar.point: Affirmative commands for tú and usted
grammar.explain: For tú, use the él / ella form of the present (cruza, sigue); for usted, swap the vowel: -ar verbs end in -e, -er and -ir verbs in -a (cruce, siga, suba).

examples.es: Cruza la calle. / Cruce la calle.

grammar.trap: The usted form looks like the 'wrong' vowel but it's right: tome, suba, baje. Strangers get usted.

grammar.explain: Some short tú commands are irregular (ven, ve, sal, haz, pon, di); the usted forms come from the yo form (venga, vaya, salga, haga, ponga, diga).

examples.es: Ve por la avenida. / Vaya por la avenida.
Sal por la otra puerta. / Salga por la otra puerta.
examples.en: Go out by the other door.

grammar.trap: ve (go!) looks like ve (he sees); context makes it clear.

grammar.point: Pronouns on the end of commands
grammar.explain: Pronouns join the end of an affirmative command, and a written accent keeps the stress where it was.

examples.en: Tell me where to get off.
Get off at the next one.
Tell me how to get there.

grammar.trap: In a command the pronoun goes on the end (avíseme), but in a question it goes first (¿me avisa?).

grammar.explain: Ir is movement away from where you are, venir towards the speaker, llegar is to arrive and regresar(se) to go back.

examples.es: Voy al centro. / ¿Vienes a mi casa?
examples.en: I'm going to the centre. / Are you coming to my place?
How do I get to the metro?

grammar.trap: When someone calls you, answer ¡Ya voy! (I'm coming), because you're going to them.

grammar.explain: Metro and Metrobús lines are named by number or colour, and the direction by the last station.
grammar.trap: transbordar is 'to change lines'; it's what signs and staff say.

pronunciation: The written accent on commands with pronouns shows where the stress stays: a-VÍ-se-me, BÁ-je-se, DÍ-ga-me.
Nahuatl station names are stressed where written: Co-yo-a-CÁN, Cha-pul-te-PEC; tl, as in Tlatelolco, is one sound.

common_errors.why: coger is vulgar in Mexico; use tomar.

common_errors.right: Avíseme dónde me bajo. / ¿Me avisa dónde me bajo?
common_errors.why: Pronouns go on the end of a command, or before the verb in a question.
recto sounds Spanish; Mexico says derecho.
billete is a banknote; a ticket is un boleto.

units.culture: Long-distance travel in Mexico is by bus: first-class lines such as ADO, ETN and Primera Plus leave from the central de autobuses, tickets are bought at the taquilla, online or in an app, and each seat has a passenger's name. On the Mexico City metro you pay a flat fare with a rechargeable card, lines are known by number, colour and end station, and the front carriages are set aside for women and children.
recycles: a1-09: ¿Dónde queda …? / Siga derecho y dé vuelta …
a1-11: ¡Bajan! / En la esquina, por favor
a1-11: tomar, never coger; Nahuatl place names
units.evidence: The learner gives a route with two or three commands in the right form for tú or usted (cruce, siga derecho, dé vuelta), asks a driver or passenger ¿me avisa dónde me bajo?, follows a metro instruction with a direction and a change, and buys a long-distance ticket, answering ¿sencillo o redondo? and asking for the andén.
sources: EeM U6 (transport, irregular imperatives), U8 (directions with read-back), U14 (¿podría decirme …?, transport)
PCIC Gram. A1 (affirmative tú imperative + di / haz / pon / sal); Func. A2 (imperatives for directions); Gén. B1 (phone to a bus station: sencillo / redondo); NG A2 (ida y vuelta → redondo)
PCIC Saberes (ADO and other lines, central de autobuses, andén; metro card)
WP (boleto, transbordar, taquilla)

units.title: Problems at home
units.can_do: Report what's broken or not working, ask the landlord to send someone, and say what happened by accident.
functions: ask when it will be done

frames.es: Se fue la luz.
frames.en: The power's gone off.
frames.note: When it comes back: Ya regresó la luz.

frames.es: No sale agua caliente.
frames.en: There's no hot water coming out.

frames.es: Se descompuso el bóiler.
frames.en: The water heater's broken.
frames.note: bóiler (also calentador) = the gas water heater.

frames.es: Hay una fuga en el baño.
frames.en: There's a leak in the bathroom.
frames.note: fuga de agua, fuga de gas.

frames.es: No sirve el contacto de la cocina.
frames.en: The socket in the kitchen doesn't work.
frames.note: no sirve = it doesn't work (everyday); no funciona also works.

frames.es: Se me rompió un vaso. / Se me cayó el celular.
frames.en: I broke a glass (by accident). / I dropped my phone.

frames.es: ¿Me puede mandar a un plomero?
frames.en: Can you send me a plumber?

frames.es: ¿Para cuándo queda?
frames.en: When will it be done?
frames.note: What you ask a repair person or a shop.

frames.es: Se acabó el gas.
frames.en: The gas has run out.
frames.note: Gas comes in a tank or a cylinder, delivered by truck.

model_exchanges.situation: A small accident at a friend's house

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Ay, perdón! Se me cayó un vaso y se rompió.
lines.en: Oh, sorry! I dropped a glass and it broke.

lines.speaker: amiga
