sources: PCIC Gén. B1 (short speeches at gatherings); Gén. C1 (formal meetings, speeches at formal events); Func. B2 and C1 5.14 (pésame); C1 5.12 (no tenías que haberte molestado → MX no te hubieras molestado); C1 5.15 (toasts)
PCIC Saberes 3.5.2–3.5.3 (weddings, padrinos, funerals), rewritten for Mexico: velorio, novenario, XV años, lo acompaño en su dolor, que en paz descanse
Word Power 6.10 (velorio, bautizo, XV años; gap: dar el pésame)

units.title: Sayings and idioms
units.can_do: Understand and use the everyday idioms and proverbs that make speech sound Mexican.
situations: encouraging a friend before an interview
admitting a mistake to a neighbour

frames.es: ¡Échale ganas!
frames.en: Give it your all!

frames.es: La regué.
frames.en: I messed up.
frames.note: regarla: always with la. Regué alone means 'I watered'.

frames.es: Me hice bolas.
frames.en: I got all mixed up.

frames.es: Ponte las pilas.
frames.en: Get your act together.
frames.note: To someone you call tú; with usted, póngase las pilas sounds bossy.

frames.es: No me quedó de otra.
frames.en: I had no other choice.

frames.es: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
frames.en: Every cloud has a silver lining.

frames.es: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente.
frames.en: You snooze, you lose.

frames.es: Más vale tarde que nunca.
frames.en: Better late than never.

frames.es: Al mal tiempo, buena cara.
frames.en: Keep smiling when things go wrong.

frames.es: Chiquito pero picoso.
frames.en: Small but fierce.
frames.note: Said of a small person, or a small chilli, that packs a punch.

model_exchanges.situation: Encouraging a friend before a job interview

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Mañana es la entrevista y estoy nerviosísima. Seguro me hago bolas.
lines.en: The interview's tomorrow and I'm so nervous. I'm bound to get all mixed up.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¡Échale ganas! Te preparaste un montón.
lines.en: Give it your all! You've prepared loads.

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Ya sé, pero la última vez la regué con la primera pregunta.
lines.en: I know, but last time I messed up the very first question.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Bueno, no hay mal que por bien no venga: ahora ya sabes qué te van a preguntar.
lines.en: Well, every cloud has a silver lining: now you know what they'll ask you.

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Tienes razón. Hoy me pongo las pilas y repaso todo.
lines.en: You're right. Today I'll get my act together and go over everything.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Así me gusta. ¡No te rajes!
lines.en: That's the spirit. Don't back out!

model_exchanges.situation: Admitting a mistake to a neighbour

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Don Toño, perdón, la regué: dejé la llave abierta y se vació el tinaco.
lines.en: Don Toño, sorry, I messed up: I left the tap on and the water tank emptied.

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: Ni modo. Al mal tiempo, buena cara. Ahorita le hablamos a la pipa.
lines.en: Oh well. Keep smiling. We'll call the water truck right now.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Me hice bolas con las llaves; no sabía cuál era cuál.
lines.en: I got mixed up with the taps; I didn't know which was which.

lines.speaker: vecino
lines.es: Les pongo una etiqueta y listo. Para la otra, ya sabe.
lines.en: I'll put a label on them and that's that. Next time, you'll know.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Gracias, don Toño. ¡Uno aprende a la mala!
lines.en: Thanks, Don Toño. You learn the hard way!

grammar.point: pronominal and clitic idioms (regarla, echarle ganas, arreglárselas, ponerse las pilas)
grammar.explain: Many Mexican idioms carry a fixed la, le, las or reflexive pronoun that refers to nothing in particular; only the person changes.

examples.en: I messed up with my landlady.
I managed as best I could.

examples.es: Ponte las pilas, que mañana es el examen.
examples.en: Get your act together, the exam's tomorrow.

grammar.trap: Keep the fixed pronoun: la regué, la regaste, la regamos. Without it the meaning changes: regué = I watered, me arreglé = I got dressed up.

grammar.explain: Proverbs are quoted whole, or just the first half (Camarón que se duerme…), and they never change tense or person.

examples.en: (You snooze…) the listener finishes it in their head.
Keep smiling when things go wrong.

grammar.trap: Don't translate English proverbs word for word: many have a different Mexican form ('You snooze, you lose' is Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente).

vocabulary.en: to put your all into it
oh well, it can't be helped

pronunciation: Proverbs fall into two halves with a short pause in the middle: Al mal tiempo, // buena cara. Camarón que se duerme // se lo lleva la corriente.
With a pronoun attached the stress stays where it was on the verb, which is why échale and ponte keep their shape: É-cha-le GA-nas, PON-te las PI-las.

common_errors.why: Without la it means 'I watered'.
The idiom is reflexive with las, not a possessive.
Arreglarse alone means to get ready or dressed up.
Proverbs are fixed; don't drop words.

units.culture: Mexicans quote dichos all the time, often only the first half, which the listener completes in their head. ¡Échale ganas! is the national encouragement, while ni modo, no hay de otra and al mal tiempo, buena cara reflect a habit of accepting what can't be changed with good humour. One well-placed saying gets a smile; a string of them sounds like a textbook.
units.evidence: In a natural moment the learner encourages someone with échale ganas or ponte las pilas, admits a mistake with la regué or me hice bolas keeping the fixed pronoun, and recognises a proverb from its first half.
sources: Seven Keys ch. 4, Table 4.1 (al mal tiempo buena cara; chiquito pero picoso; fatalistic proverbs)
PCIC Saberes 3.1.1 (proverbs that carry shared attitudes), rewritten for Mexico; Nociones generales C2 6.6 (meter la pata → MX regarla); Nociones generales C1 6.9 (liarse → MX hacerse bolas)

PCIC Gram. C1 (fixed clitic expressions: arreglárselas, fastidiarla → MX regarla); Func. C1–C2 (no me queda de otra; No hay mal que por bien no venga); Func. C1 4.25 (encouragement → MX ¡Échale ganas!)

units.title: Arts, literature and cinema
units.can_do: Discuss Mexican books, art, music and films: what they're about, what they mean, and what you think.

frames.es: Estoy leyendo Pedro Páramo y me cuesta trabajo seguirle el hilo.
frames.en: I'm reading Pedro Páramo and I'm finding it hard to follow.

frames.es: Es una novela en la que casi todos los personajes ya están muertos.
frames.en: It's a novel in which almost all the characters are already dead.

frames.es: Me fascina cómo Rulfo cuenta las cosas sin decirlas.
frames.en: I love how Rulfo tells things without saying them.

frames.es: Lo que más me llamó la atención fue el final.
frames.en: What struck me most was the ending.

frames.es: Rulfo, cuya obra es muy breve, sigue siendo de los autores más leídos.
frames.en: Rulfo, whose work is very short, is still one of the most widely read authors.

frames.es: Los murales de Rivera en Palacio Nacional cuentan la historia del país.
frames.en: Rivera's murals in the National Palace tell the country's history.

frames.es: La obra de Frida Kahlo habla mucho del dolor y de la identidad.
frames.en: Frida Kahlo's work says a lot about pain and identity.

frames.es: ¿Has visto alguna película de la Época de Oro?
frames.en: Have you seen any films from the golden age?
frames.note: Mexican cinema's golden age, roughly the 1930s to the 1950s: Pedro Infante, María Félix, Cantinflas.

frames.es: ¿Me recomiendas algo de Rosario Castellanos para empezar?
frames.en: Can you recommend something by Rosario Castellanos to start with?

model_exchanges.situation: A book club

lines.speaker: moderadora
lines.es: ¿Qué les pareció Pedro Páramo?
lines.en: What did you think of Pedro Páramo?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Al principio me costó trabajo seguirle el hilo. No sabía quién estaba vivo y quién muerto.
lines.en: At first I found it hard to follow. I didn't know who was alive and who was dead.

lines.speaker: lector
lines.es: Esa es la gracia. Es una novela en la que casi todos ya están muertos.
lines.en: That's the beauty of it. It's a novel in which almost everyone is already dead.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Ahora lo entiendo. Me fascina cómo Rulfo cuenta las cosas sin decirlas.
lines.en: Now I get it. I love how Rulfo tells things without saying them.

lines.speaker: moderadora
lines.es: ¿Y qué fue lo que más te llamó la atención?
lines.en: And what struck you most?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: El final. Lo tuve que leer dos veces.
lines.en: The ending. I had to read it twice.

model_exchanges.situation: A film night with friends

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: Hoy toca Nosotros los pobres. ¿Has visto alguna película de la Época de Oro?
lines.en: Tonight it's Nosotros los pobres. Have you seen any golden-age films?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Solo una de Cantinflas, y no le entendí la mitad de los chistes.
lines.en: Just one with Cantinflas, and I didn't get half the jokes.

lines.speaker: amiga
lines.es: Normal: Cantinflas habla mucho sin decir nada. De ahí viene «cantinflear».
lines.en: That's normal: Cantinflas talks a lot without saying anything. That's where 'cantinflear' comes from.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Y Pedro Infante? Todo el mundo habla de él.
lines.en: And Pedro Infante? Everyone talks about him.

lines.speaker: amigo
lines.es: Era el ídolo de mis abuelos. Ya verás: al final vas a llorar.
lines.en: He was my grandparents' idol. You'll see: you'll be crying by the end.

model_exchanges.situation: With a guide at an art museum

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Este autorretrato de Frida es original?
lines.en: Is this self-portrait by Frida an original?

lines.speaker: guía
lines.es: Sí. Fíjese en los detalles: su obra habla mucho del dolor y de la identidad.
lines.en: Yes. Look at the details: her work says a lot about pain and identity.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿Y Diego Rivera pintaba también cuadros, o solo murales?
lines.en: And did Diego Rivera also paint canvases, or only murals?

lines.speaker: guía
lines.es: Las dos cosas, pero los muralistas querían el arte en los muros públicos, para que todo el pueblo lo viera.
lines.en: Both, but the muralists wanted art on public walls, so that everyone could see it.

grammar.explain: Cuyo (whose) agrees with the thing owned, and el cual / la cual is a careful 'which' or 'who', used mostly after prepositions.

examples.es: una autora cuya obra se lee en todo el mundo
examples.en: an author whose work is read all over the world

examples.es: la casa en la cual vivió Frida
examples.en: the house in which Frida lived

examples.es: Rivera pintó el mural, el cual tardó años en terminar.
examples.en: Rivera painted the mural, which took years to finish.

grammar.trap: In conversation Mexicans mostly use que and en la que; cuyo and el cual belong to careful speech, reviews and writing.

grammar.explain: When a relative follows a preposition, Spanish uses article + que (en la que, con el que, por la que), and the preposition always comes first.

examples.es: Es una novela en la que los muertos hablan.
examples.en: It's a novel in which the dead talk.

examples.es: la película de la que te hablé
examples.en: the film I told you about

examples.es: la razón por la que me gusta
examples.en: the reason why I like it

grammar.trap: English can end with the preposition ('the film I told you about'); Spanish moves it to the front: la película de la que te hablé.

grammar.explain: A small set of verbs and nouns covers most talk about a work: tratar de, contar, retratar, la trama, el personaje, el ritmo, el final.

examples.es: Trata de un hombre que busca a su padre.
examples.en: It's about a man looking for his father.

examples.es: Retrata muy bien la vida en el campo.
examples.en: It portrays country life very well.

examples.es: El ritmo es lento, pero vale la pena.
examples.en: It's slow, but it's worth it.

grammar.trap: False friends: el argumento is the plot, not an argument, and una película actual is a current film, not one based on fact.

vocabulary.en: the golden age of Mexican cinema
to talk a lot without saying anything

pronunciation: Names keep their Spanish stress: RUL-fo, PÁ-ra-mo, Sor JUA-na. In Kahlo the h is silent: KA-lo.
Watch the stress shift between related words: pintor, pintura; música, músico, musical. The written accent tells you where it falls.

common_errors.wrong: la película que te hablé de
common_errors.right: la película de la que te hablé
common_errors.why: The preposition goes before the relative.

common_errors.wrong: Lo más que me gustó fue el final.
common_errors.right: Lo que más me gustó fue el final.
common_errors.why: más goes after lo que, before the verb.

common_errors.wrong: Es una película muy actual. (meaning based on fact)
common_errors.right: Está basada en una historia real.
common_errors.why: actual means current.
The h is silent.

units.culture: Mexicans are proud of their arts and generous with recommendations. The muralists (Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros) put national history on public walls, Frida Kahlo is a national icon, and Rulfo, Paz, Sor Juana and Rosario Castellanos are read at school. Golden-age films still show on television, and quoting Cantinflas or Pedro Infante is everyday shorthand. Many museums are free on Sundays for Mexicans and foreign residents.
recycles: b2-13 (Se trata de una familia que… Está basada en una historia real. ¿La viste doblada o subtitulada?)
units.evidence: Talking about a book, film or artwork, the learner says what it's about with tratar de, gives a reasoned opinion with lo que más me llamó la atención…, uses a relative with a preposition correctly, and asks for or gives a recommendation.
sources: PCIC Referentes culturales (Paz, Rulfo / Comala, the muralists, Kahlo, corrido / danzón / ranchera, golden age of cinema; Cantinflas missing); Gén. C1 (novels, reviews)
PCIC Gram. C1 (cuyo, el cual; relatives with prepositions); Nociones específicas C1 18 (obra maestra, trama, peliculón)
Seven Keys ch. 2 and 3 (murals; golden-age cinema: Pedro Infante, María Félix, Cantinflas)

units.title: Community life and mediation
units.can_do: Clear up misunderstandings, explain what someone meant, and help newcomers and Mexicans understand each other.

frames.es: Perdón, creo que hubo un malentendido.
frames.en: Sorry, I think there's been a misunderstanding.

frames.es: Lo que quiso decir es que no está de acuerdo con la cuota.
frames.en: What she meant is that she doesn't agree with the fee.

frames.es: Ella se refiere a que nadie le avisó de la junta.
frames.en: What she's getting at is that nobody told her about the meeting.

frames.es: En otras palabras, no es que no quiera pagar, es que no le alcanza.
frames.en: In other words, it's not that she doesn't want to pay; she can't afford it.

frames.es: No lo tomes a mal, pero aquí eso se considera grosero.
frames.en: Don't take it the wrong way, but that's considered rude here.

frames.es: ¿Me ayudas a explicarle a la señora lo que pasó?
frames.en: Will you help me explain to the lady what happened?

frames.es: Aquí se acostumbra saludar a todos al llegar.
frames.en: Here it's usual to greet everyone when you arrive.

frames.es: O sea, no es por conocerlos, es por respeto.
frames.en: I mean, it's not because you know them; it's out of respect.

model_exchanges.situation: A residents' meeting: helping a new neighbour and the administrator understand each other

lines.speaker: administradora
lines.es: La cuota de mantenimiento sube a mil doscientos a partir de enero.
lines.en: The maintenance fee goes up to twelve hundred from January.

lines.speaker: vecina nueva
lines.es: No… no estoy… ¿cómo se dice? No me parece.
lines.en: No… I'm not… how do you say it? I don't think that's right.

lines.speaker: administradora
lines.es: ¿Cómo que no le parece? Lo votamos en la junta.
lines.en: What do you mean you don't think it's right? We voted on it at the meeting.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Perdón, creo que hubo un malentendido. Lo que quiso decir es que no está de acuerdo, porque no vino a la junta.
lines.en: Sorry, I think there's been a misunderstanding. What she meant is that she doesn't agree, because she didn't come to the meeting.

lines.speaker: administradora
lines.es: Ah, ya. Pero la junta se avisó por el grupo de WhatsApp.
lines.en: Oh, I see. But the meeting was announced on the WhatsApp group.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: En otras palabras, ella no está en el grupo. ¿La podemos agregar?
lines.en: In other words, she isn't in the group. Can we add her?

lines.speaker: administradora
lines.es: Claro que sí. Ahorita la agrego.
lines.en: Of course. I'll add her right now.

model_exchanges.situation: Explaining a custom to a new arrival

lines.speaker: recién llegado
lines.es: Ayer entré a la oficina y la señora de la recepción me vio feo. ¿Hice algo mal?
lines.en: Yesterday I walked into the office and the receptionist gave me a dirty look. Did I do something wrong?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: ¿La saludaste al entrar?
lines.en: Did you say hello to her when you went in?

lines.speaker: recién llegado
lines.es: No, fui directo al elevador.
lines.en: No, I went straight to the lift.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: No lo tomes a mal, pero aquí eso se considera grosero. Aquí se acostumbra saludar a todos al llegar.
lines.en: Don't take it the wrong way, but that's considered rude here. Here it's usual to greet everyone when you arrive.

lines.speaker: recién llegado
lines.es: ¿Aunque no los conozca?
lines.en: Even if I don't know them?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.es: Sí: buenos días a la señora, al guardia, a quien esté. O sea, no es por conocerlos, es por respeto.
lines.en: Yes: good morning to the receptionist, the guard, whoever's there. I mean, it's not because you know them; it's out of respect.

grammar.point: reformulation: o sea, es decir, en otras palabras, lo que quiso decir
grammar.explain: These markers introduce a clearer version of what was just said, by you or by someone else.

examples.en: So, in other words, he's not coming.

examples.es: Es decir, hay que pagar antes del cinco.
examples.en: That is, you have to pay before the fifth.

examples.es: Lo que quiso decir es que necesita más tiempo.
examples.en: What he meant is that he needs more time.

grammar.trap: Lo que quiso decir needs es que: lo que quiso decir es que…, not lo que quiso decir que…

grammar.explain: To pass on what someone said, shift the tense back after a past verb, and use the subjunctive for requests.

examples.es: Dice que no está de acuerdo con la cuota.
examples.en: She says she doesn't agree with the fee.

examples.es: Dijo que no podía pagar este mes.
examples.en: She said she couldn't pay this month.

examples.es: Le pidió que esperara hasta el viernes.
examples.en: She asked him to wait until Friday.

grammar.trap: After pidió que or dijo que (for a request), the verb is in the past subjunctive: que esperara, not que espera.

grammar.explain: A mediator often uses usted with one person and tú with another in the same conversation, and has to keep each person's form straight.

examples.es: Señora, ¿me permite? Ella se refiere a que usted no le avisó.
examples.en: Señora, may I? What she means is that you didn't tell her. (usted)

examples.es: Oye, lo que dice la señora es que la junta fue el martes.
examples.en: Listen, what the lady's saying is that the meeting was on Tuesday. (tú)

grammar.trap: Don't mix forms when talking to the same person (usted… te…); decide for each person and stick to it.

vocabulary.en: to be in the habit of (se acostumbra = it's the custom); acostumbrarse = to get used to
I mean, so, in other words
to give someone a dirty look

pronunciation: When you rephrase for someone, slow down and stress the key word: lo que quiso decir es que NO está de acuerdo.
O sea runs together, almost as two syllables (o-SEA); in fast speech it's also a filler, and Mexicans can tell a clarifying o sea from a hesitating one by the pause after it.

common_errors.wrong: Lo que ella quiso decir que…
common_errors.right: Lo que quiso decir es que…
common_errors.why: The cleft needs es que.
referirse takes a.
A reported request takes the past subjunctive.
A negative command uses the subjunctive, and the phrase is tomar a mal.

units.culture: Mexicans readily forgive a newcomer's grammar, but social slips less: not greeting a room, skipping usted with an older person, being curt at a meeting. After a while here you'll be the one explaining these customs to new arrivals, and smoothing things over when Mexicans misread a foreigner's directness. Do it privately and kindly: correcting someone in public makes them lose face.
recycles: b2-07 (No quise ser grosero. Se me hace que no le gustó la idea.)
c1-05 (No es que…, sino que…; Con todo respeto…)
b2-05 (cuota, junta de vecinos, WhatsApp group)
units.evidence: In a three-way conversation, the learner spots a misunderstanding, rephrases what one person meant for the other with lo que quiso decir es que or en otras palabras, keeps tú and usted straight with each person, and explains a Mexican custom tactfully.
sources: PCIC Habilidades y actitudes interculturales 3–4 (interaction and cultural mediation: reformulate what could cause a misunderstanding; make implicit cultural points explicit); Obj. C2 (mediation); Proc. 1.4.2 (reformulating to confirm: es decir que…, o sea que…)
PCIC Saberes 3.4 (tolerance of foreigners' errors by type) and 2.1.5 (greeting strangers on entering), rewritten for Mexico
PCIC Tác. C1 1.2 (reformulators: dicho de otro modo, en resumidas cuentas)
Seven Keys ch. 4 (play the foreigner card; criticise in private, praise in public)

grammar_inventory.title: Afuera grammar inventory: Mexican Spanish A1–C1
grammar_inventory.author: Magda
grammar_inventory.about: Every grammar point in the A1–C1 outline (outline.json), at the unit where the outline teaches it, grouped by part of speech and in teaching order within each group (outline unit order). Points the outline implies but never names are added at the unit that first needs them. Mexican usage throughout: ustedes (vosotros recognised at C1 only), the preterite for today and with ya, lo / la for people and things (le only for formal usted), ir a + infinitive as the everyday future and the synthetic future mainly for guesses, accidental se from A1 as a chunk, -ra imperfect subjunctive, si hubiera … hubiera. use = "say" means the learner produces it at that unit; "understand" means recognise only. explain is one plain English sentence; trap is the mistake English speakers make; example is a Mexican sentence with its English.

points.point: un / una / unos / unas: the indefinite article shows the noun's gender (un taco, una quesadilla, unos tacos)
points.explain: 'A' is un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine one; unos / unas mean 'some'.
points.trap: English has one 'a', so learners forget that the noun's gender picks the article.

example.es: Me da una quesadilla y unos tacos de pastor, por favor.
example.en: Can I have a quesadilla and some al pastor tacos, please?

points.point: el / un before feminine nouns that start with a stressed a- (el agua, un agua de horchata)
points.explain: Feminine nouns beginning with a stressed a- take el / un in the singular but stay feminine.
points.trap: Hearing el agua, learners make the noun masculine: it's el agua fría and las aguas frescas.

example.es: Un agua de jamaica bien fría, por favor.
example.en: A really cold jamaica water, please.

points.point: el / la / los / las for something specific; el de, la roja for 'the one'
points.explain: The definite article marks something specific, and with de or an adjective it stands for a noun already mentioned: el de allá = the one over there.
points.trap: Spanish has no word for 'one' here: el de allá, la roja, not *el uno de allá.

example.es: ¿Me da ese, por favor? El de allá.
example.en: Can I have that one, please? The one over there.

points.point: contractions al (a + el) and del (de + el)
points.explain: A and de join with el to make al and del; they never join with la, los or las.
points.trap: Learners write *a el or *de el, or contract with la (*dela).

example.es: Está al lado del banco, en la esquina.
example.en: It's next to the bank, on the corner.

points.point: hay + un / una (or no article), never hay + el / la
points.explain: Hay introduces something new, so it takes un / una, a number or no article; something already known takes el / la + está.
points.trap: *Hay el cajero is wrong: say hay un cajero or el cajero está…

example.es: ¿Hay un cajero por aquí? — Sí, el cajero está en la esquina.
example.en: Is there an ATM around here? — Yes, the ATM is on the corner.

points.point: days with el and no preposition: el sábado = on Saturday, los sábados = on Saturdays
points.explain: A day with el means this coming one; with los it means every week.
points.trap: There's no word for 'on': *en sábado is wrong.

example.es: ¿Nos vemos el sábado? Los sábados no trabajo.
example.en: Shall we meet on Saturday? I don't work on Saturdays.

points.point: la / las with clock time: a la una, a las cinco
points.explain: Clock times always take la or las, because hora is understood.
points.trap: English 'at five' has no article: *a cinco is wrong.

example.es: Abren a las nueve y cierran a la una.
example.en: They open at nine and close at one.

points.point: the definite article with general nouns and with the subject of gustar (me gusta la comida)
points.explain: When you talk about something in general, or about what you like, the noun takes el / la / los / las.
points.trap: English says 'I like Mexican food' with no article; Spanish needs one: me gusta la comida mexicana.

example.es: Me encantan los tamales y me gusta mucho el mole.
example.en: I love tamales and I really like mole.

points.point: the article, not a possessive, with parts of the body (me duele la cabeza)
points.explain: With body parts Spanish uses el / la, because me already says whose they are.
points.trap: *Me duele mi cabeza sounds as if you had a spare head.

example.es: Me duele la cabeza y tengo un poco de calentura.
example.en: I've got a headache and a bit of a temperature.

points.point: a la casa = home (Mexico): me voy a la casa, estoy en la casa
points.explain: In Mexico 'home' is usually la casa with the article; a casa without it is also understood.
points.trap: English 'home' has no article, and Spain-based books drop it; in Mexico ya me voy a la casa is normal.

example.es: Ya me voy a la casa, mañana nos vemos.
example.en: I'm heading home now, see you tomorrow.

points.point: titles: article when you talk about someone (la licenciada Ruiz), none when you address them (Buenos días, licenciada)
points.explain: Señor, licenciada, doctor and the like take el / la when you mention the person, and no article when you speak to them.
points.trap: *Buenos días, la licenciada is wrong; *¿Se encuentra licenciada Ruiz? sounds clipped.

example.es: ¿Se encuentra la licenciada Ruiz? — Ella habla. — Buenos días, licenciada.
example.en: Is Ms Ruiz there? — Speaking. — Good morning.

points.point: no article with a job after ser (es contadora); un / una only with an adjective (es una contadora muy buena)
points.explain: After ser, a job, nationality or religion takes no article unless an adjective follows.
points.trap: English 'she's an accountant' tempts *es una contadora.

example.es: Mi vecina es contadora; es una contadora muy buena.
example.en: My neighbour is an accountant; she's a very good accountant.

points.point: lo + adjective and lo que (lo bueno, lo que más me gusta)
points.explain: Lo with an adjective means 'the … thing', and lo que means 'what' in the middle of a sentence.
points.trap: English 'what' tempts *qué (lo que is needed) and 'the good thing' tempts *el bueno.

example.es: Lo que más me gusta de aquí es la gente; lo malo es el tráfico.
example.en: What I like most here is the people; the bad thing is the traffic.

points.point: the emphatic article and lo + adjective + que in exclamations (¡la cara que puso!, ¡lo caro que está todo!)
points.explain: An exclamation can be built from el / la or lo + adjective + que to stress how extreme something was.
points.trap: It looks like an unfinished sentence; it's complete and means 'what a…!' or 'how…!'.

example.es: ¡No sabes la cara que puso! ¡Y lo caro que estaba!
example.en: You should have seen his face! And how expensive it was!

points.point: the diminutive -ito / -ita as a softener (un momentito, un poquito, ahorita)
points.explain: -ito makes a word smaller or kinder; in Mexico it softens requests and time.
points.trap: It doesn't always mean small: un cafecito is just a coffee offered warmly.

example.es: Un momentito, por favor, ahorita lo atiendo.
example.en: Just a moment, please, I'll be with you right away.

points.point: every noun is masculine or feminine; most -o nouns are masculine, most -a nouns feminine
points.explain: Learn each noun with el or la: el taco, la tortilla, el café, la leche.
points.trap: Endings mislead: el día, el mapa, la mano, la foto.

example.es: El café está caliente y la leche está fría.
example.en: The coffee is hot and the milk is cold.

points.point: plurals: -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant, -z → -ces
points.explain: Add -s to nouns ending in a vowel and -es to nouns ending in a consonant; a final -z becomes -ces.
points.trap: Written accents move: limón → limones, joven → jóvenes, lápiz → lápices.

example.es: Dos limones y tres tortas, por favor.
example.en: Two limes and three tortas, please.

points.point: noun + de + noun for fillings, flavours and kinds (tacos de pastor, agua de jamaica)
points.explain: Spanish describes a noun with de + another noun after it.
points.trap: English puts the describing noun first ('pastor tacos'); Spanish reverses it.

example.es: Tres tacos de suadero y un agua de horchata.
example.en: Three suadero tacos and an horchata.

points.point: drinks and foods become countable when you order (un café, dos aguas, tres cocas)
points.explain: When ordering, a mass noun counts as a cup, bottle or portion: un café = a coffee.
points.trap: Learners add a container word every time; dos aguas is enough.

example.es: Dos aguas naturales y un café americano.
example.en: Two still waters and an americano.

points.point: -ito for size and warmth, with spelling changes (chico → chiquito, poco → poquito, casa → casita)
points.explain: The diminutive also means small or dear; c becomes qu and z becomes c before -ito.
points.trap: *chicito and *pocito are wrong spellings.

example.es: Tiene dos recámaras y una cocina chiquita.
example.en: It has two bedrooms and a tiny kitchen.

points.point: -ma nouns from Greek are masculine (el clima, el problema, el tema)
points.explain: Many nouns in -ma are masculine: el clima, el problema, el programa, el tema.
points.trap: The -a ending makes learners say *la clima, *la problema.

example.es: El clima aquí es muy agradable.
example.en: The weather here is very pleasant.

points.point: masculine plural for mixed groups: mis papás = my parents, mis hermanos = my brothers and sisters
points.explain: A masculine plural covers a mixed group; papás is the everyday word for parents.
points.trap: Hermanos can include sisters, and hijos can include daughters.

example.es: Mis papás viven en Toronto y mis hermanos en Chicago.
example.en: My parents live in Toronto and my brothers and sisters in Chicago.

points.point: nouns used in the plural for one thing (los lentes, los pantalones, las tijeras, las ganas)
points.explain: Some single objects are plural in Spanish, so their articles and adjectives are plural too.
points.trap: *mi lente nuevo for 'my new glasses': say mis lentes nuevos.

example.es: ¿Has visto mis lentes? No los encuentro.
example.en: Have you seen my glasses? I can't find them.

points.point: collective nouns take a singular verb (la gente es muy amable)
points.explain: Gente, familia and similar nouns are grammatically singular.
points.trap: English 'people are' tempts *la gente son.

example.es: La gente de esta colonia es muy amable.
example.en: The people in this neighbourhood are very friendly.

points.point: nouns in -ción, -dad, -miento for a formal, nominal style (la entrega, la solicitud, el cumplimiento)
points.explain: Formal writing turns verbs into nouns: entregar → la entrega, cumplir → el cumplimiento.
points.trap: Translating English verb phrases word for word sounds too chatty in a formal letter.

example.es: Le agradezco la revisión de mi solicitud y su pronta respuesta.
example.en: Thank you for reviewing my application and for your prompt reply.

points.point: augmentatives -ote / -ota, -ón and -azo (grandote, un calorón, un golpazo)
points.explain: These endings make things bigger, stronger or rougher, often with humour.
points.trap: -azo can also mean a blow: un codazo is a nudge with the elbow, not a big elbow.

example.es: ¡Qué calorón! Y el perro de tu vecino está grandote.
example.en: What a scorcher! And your neighbour's dog is huge.

points.point: nouns whose meaning changes with gender (el capital / la capital, el orden / la orden, el corte / la corte)
points.explain: A few nouns mean different things in the masculine and the feminine.
points.trap: Mixing them up changes the meaning: la orden is an order (command or food order), el orden is tidiness.

example.es: Sin el capital no podemos abrir el negocio en la capital.
example.en: Without the capital we can't open the business in the capital city.

points.point: Nahuatl loanwords and the -te ending (aguacate, chocolate, cacahuate, tianguis)
points.explain: Many everyday Mexican words come from Nahuatl, often ending in -te from Nahuatl -tl.
points.trap: They're not slang: they're the standard Mexican words.

example.es: Aguacate, chocolate y cacahuate vienen del náhuatl.
example.en: Avocado, chocolate and peanut come from Nahuatl.

points.point: descriptive and colour adjectives go after the noun (salsa verde, agua natural)
points.explain: Most adjectives that describe or classify follow the noun.
points.trap: English order (green salsa) leads to *verde salsa.

example.es: ¿La salsa verde pica más que la roja?
example.en: Is the green salsa hotter than the red one?

points.point: numbers to 1,000 for prices; cien vs ciento; quinientos, setecientos, novecientos
points.explain: 100 on its own is cien; from 101 it's ciento: ciento veinte. 500, 700 and 900 are irregular.
points.trap: *cinco cientos, *siete cientos, and *un mil (just mil).

example.es: Son trescientos cincuenta pesos; la otra cuesta quinientos.
example.en: That's 350 pesos; the other one is 500.

points.point: hundreds agree with the noun (doscientos pesos, doscientas personas)
points.explain: From 200 to 900, the hundreds change for feminine nouns.
points.trap: Learners never change numbers in English, so they say *doscientos personas.

example.es: Había como doscientas personas en la fila.
example.en: There were about two hundred people in the queue.

points.point: prices and phone numbers in Mexico: $85.50, $1,250; ten-digit numbers read in pairs
points.explain: Mexico writes a decimal point and a thousands comma, as in the US, and reads phone numbers two digits at a time.
points.trap: Spain-based books write 1.250,50 and group phone numbers differently.

example.es: Mi celular es el cincuenta y cinco, doce, treinta y cuatro, cincuenta y seis, setenta y ocho.
example.en: My mobile is 55 12 34 56 78.

points.point: demonstratives este / ese / aquel and neuter esto / eso / aquello
points.explain: Este is near me, ese near you or a bit away, aquel far away; esto / eso point at something you don't name.
points.trap: Esto and eso never go before a noun: *esto pan → este pan.

example.es: ¿Cuánto cuesta este? ¿Y eso qué es?
example.en: How much is this one? And what's that?

points.point: otro / otra without un (otro taco, otra vez)
points.explain: Otro already includes 'an', so it takes no article.
points.trap: English 'another' tempts *un otro.

example.es: ¿Me da otro, por favor?
example.en: Can I have another one, please?

points.point: quantities with de: medio kilo de, un cuarto de, un kilo de, doscientos gramos de
points.explain: Weights and portions link to the food with de.
points.trap: *un medio kilo is wrong: medio takes no article.

example.es: Deme medio kilo de jitomate y un cuarto de queso.
example.en: Give me half a kilo of tomatoes and a quarter of cheese.

points.point: possessives mi / tu / su (+ -s in the plural)
points.explain: Mi, tu and su go before the noun and add -s for plural things; su can mean his, her, its, your (usted) or their.
points.trap: The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: mis llaves, even if 'I' am one person.

example.es: Mi casero vive abajo con su familia; sus hijos son muy amables.
example.en: My landlord lives downstairs with his family; his children are very kind.

points.point: ordinals 1st–10th; primer / tercer before a masculine noun; planta baja vs primer piso
points.explain: Primero and tercero drop the -o before a masculine noun; in Mexico planta baja is the ground floor and primer piso is one floor up.
points.trap: US learners count the ground floor as the first floor and go one floor too low.

example.es: Vivo en el tercer piso, y la lavandería está en la planta baja.
example.en: I live on the third floor, and the laundry is on the ground floor.

points.point: mucho / poco agree with the noun (mucho calor, muchas cosas, poca gente)
points.explain: Before a noun, mucho and poco agree like any adjective.
points.trap: *muchos gente: gente is singular, so it's mucha gente.

example.es: Hoy hace mucho calor y hay poca gente en la calle.
example.en: It's very hot today and there aren't many people in the street.

points.point: buen / mal before a masculine singular noun (hace buen tiempo, un buen lugar)
points.explain: Bueno and malo drop the -o before a masculine singular noun.
points.trap: *un bueno lugar sounds wrong; after the noun it stays bueno: un lugar bueno.

example.es: Hoy hace buen tiempo para ir al mercado.
example.en: The weather's good today for going to the market.

points.point: adjective agreement in gender and number (alto / alta / altos / altas; amable doesn't change for gender)
points.explain: Adjectives agree with the noun; those ending in -e or a consonant only change for plural.
points.trap: Learners describing a woman forget -a: *mi hermana es alto.

example.es: Mi hermana es alta y muy simpática; mis primos también son altos.
example.en: My sister is tall and very nice; my cousins are tall too.

points.point: nuestro / nuestra; su clarified with de usted / de él when needed
points.explain: Nuestro agrees with the thing owned; because su has many meanings, Mexicans add de él, de ella or de usted to be clear.
points.trap: Su familia with an older person is heard as 'your family' (usted), not 'his family'.

example.es: Nuestro depa es chiquito. ¿Y la casa de ustedes?
example.en: Our flat is tiny. What about your house?

points.point: -ísimo for 'really' (riquísimo, buenísimo, carísimo)
points.explain: Add -ísimo to the adjective without its last vowel to make it stronger.
points.trap: Spelling changes: rico → riquísimo, largo → larguísimo.

example.es: ¡Estuvo riquísimo, gracias!
example.en: That was delicious, thank you!

points.point: comparatives más / menos … que; más de / menos de with numbers
points.explain: Comparing uses más or menos + adjective + que; before a number it's de.
points.trap: *más que 500 pesos: with numbers it's más de 500 pesos.

example.es: Esta chamarra es más cara que la otra; cuesta más de mil pesos.
example.en: This jacket is more expensive than the other one; it costs over a thousand pesos.

points.point: colours agree (playeras rojas), but colour nouns don't (playeras rosa, naranja, café)
points.explain: Ordinary colour adjectives agree; colours named after things usually stay the same.
points.trap: Café means brown in Mexico (ojos cafés); marrón sounds Spanish.

example.es: Busco unos tenis negros y una playera café.
example.en: I'm looking for black trainers and a brown T-shirt.

points.point: dates: el + number + de + month; primero for the 1st; hoy es 15
points.explain: Dates use ordinary numbers except primero for the first; Mexicans say hoy es 15.
points.trap: Spain's estamos a 15 sounds odd in Mexico; *el quinceavo is wrong.

example.es: Hoy es 15. Quisiera una cita para el jueves 22, o el primero de mayo.
example.en: Today's the 15th. I'd like an appointment for Thursday the 22nd, or the 1st of May.

points.point: superlative el / la / los / las más … de (la mejor taquería de la colonia)
points.explain: The superlative is el más + adjective, and the group comes after de.
points.trap: English 'in' tempts *la mejor en la colonia.

example.es: Es la mejor taquería de la colonia.
example.en: It's the best taco place in the neighbourhood.

points.point: mejor, peor, mayor, menor; más grande / más chico for size
points.explain: Bueno and malo have irregular comparatives; mayor and menor are mostly for age.
points.trap: *más bueno instead of mejor; and mayor = older, not 'bigger' for things.

example.es: Mi hermano menor vive en una casa más grande que la mía.
example.en: My younger brother lives in a bigger house than mine.

points.point: tan … como and tanto / tanta / tantos / tantas … como
points.explain: Equality is tan + adjective + como, or tanto + noun + como (agreeing).
points.trap: *tan … que for 'as … as'.

example.es: No es tan caro como pensaba, y no hay tanto tráfico como en el centro.
example.en: It's not as expensive as I thought, and there isn't as much traffic as downtown.

points.point: stressed possessives mío, tuyo, suyo and el mío / la tuya
points.explain: After ser, or with the article to replace a noun, use mío, tuyo, suyo, agreeing with the thing.
points.trap: *Este es mi is wrong: este es mío / es el mío.

example.es: Tu colonia es más tranquila que la mía.
example.en: Your neighbourhood is quieter than mine.

points.point: adjective + de + infinitive (difícil de creer, fácil de usar)
points.explain: After an adjective, de + infinitive says what something is hard or easy to do.
points.trap: *difícil para creer.

example.es: Lo que me contaste es difícil de creer.
example.en: What you told me is hard to believe.

points.point: adjectives that change meaning with position (un viejo amigo / un amigo viejo, un gran pueblo / un pueblo grande, pobre)
points.explain: Before the noun some adjectives are subjective (a long-standing friend, a great town); after it they are literal.
points.trap: Putting viejo first is fine about a friendship but rude if you mean the person is old.

example.es: Es un viejo amigo, no un amigo viejo.
example.en: He's a friend of many years, not an old friend.

points.point: classifying adjectives after the noun for precise description (dolor punzante, sordo, agudo, constante)
points.explain: Precise adjectives after the noun narrow down the kind of pain, problem or thing.
points.trap: English stacks adjectives before the noun; Spanish puts them after, joined by y if there are two.

example.es: Es un dolor punzante y constante, aquí, del lado derecho.
example.en: It's a sharp, constant pain, here, on the right side.

parts_of_speech.name: Pronouns (subject, object, usted / ustedes, relatives, interrogatives)

points.point: usted and tú: usted takes the third-person verb (¿Cómo está? / ¿Cómo estás?)
points.explain: Usted is 'you' with a verb in the él / ella form; tú has its own form ending in -s.
points.trap: Mixing the two: *¿Usted estás bien?

example.es: Buenos días, señora. ¿Cómo está?
example.en: Good morning. How are you?

points.point: ustedes for any group, friends included; vosotros isn't used in Mexico
points.explain: Ustedes is the only plural 'you' in Mexico and takes the ellos / ellas form.
points.trap: Spain-based books teach vosotros; Mexicans never use it.

example.es: ¡Buenas tardes a todos! ¿Cómo están?
example.en: Good afternoon, everyone! How are you?

points.point: lo = 'it' inside fixed chunks (¿Me lo puede repetir?)
points.explain: Lo stands for 'it' and goes before the conjugated verb.
points.trap: English word order gives *¿Puede repetir lo?

example.es: Perdón, ¿me lo puede repetir más despacio?
example.en: Sorry, could you repeat that more slowly?

points.point: subject pronouns are usually dropped; use them for contrast (… ¿y usted?)
points.explain: The verb ending already shows who; yo, tú, usted are added for contrast or politeness.
points.trap: Saying yo in every sentence sounds heavy or insistent.

example.es: Vivo aquí, en la colonia. ¿Y usted?
example.en: I live here, in the neighbourhood. And you?

points.point: cuánto / cuánta / cuántos / cuántas agree with the noun
points.explain: Before a noun, cuánto agrees; on its own with a verb it stays cuánto.
points.trap: *¿Cuánto tortillas?

example.es: ¿Cuánto es? ¿Y cuántas tortillas le doy?
example.en: How much is it? And how many tortillas shall I give you?

points.point: me lo llevo / me la llevo as a chunk; the pronoun matches the thing
points.explain: Me lo llevo means 'I'll take it'; lo or la agrees with what you're buying.
points.trap: Learners say me lo llevo for everything: a bag (la bolsa) is me la llevo.

example.es: Esta bolsa está bonita. Me la llevo.
example.en: This bag is nice. I'll take it.

points.point: me / te / le with gustar, and a mí / a ti / a usted for emphasis
points.explain: With gustar the person is an indirect object (me, te, le); a mí, a ti, a usted add emphasis.
points.trap: *Yo gusto el mole, and *A mí gusta (the me is still needed).

example.es: A mí me encanta el mole. ¿Y a usted?
example.en: I love mole. What about you?

points.point: a mí también / a mí tampoco / a mí sí / a mí no to agree or disagree about likes
points.explain: After a gustar sentence, agree with a mí también (or tampoco after a negative) and disagree with a mí sí / a mí no.
points.trap: Yo también is for ordinary verbs; after no me gusta it must be tampoco.

example.es: —No me gusta el picante. —A mí tampoco.
example.en: —I don't like spicy food. —Neither do I.

points.point: direct object pronouns lo / la / los / las; Mexico uses lo / la for people too, not le
points.explain: Lo, la, los, las replace a thing or person that receives the action, agreeing in gender and number.
points.trap: Spain-based books allow le for 'him' (le vi); in Mexico say lo vi.

example.es: ¿La chamarra? Me la llevo. ¿Y a tu primo? No lo conozco.
example.en: The jacket? I'll take it. And your cousin? I don't know him.

points.point: pronoun position: before the conjugated verb or attached to an infinitive (¿Me la puedo probar? / ¿Puedo probármela?)
points.explain: With verb + infinitive the pronouns go before the first verb or on the end of the infinitive.
points.trap: Attaching adds a written accent (probármela) and the pronouns never split: *me puedo probarla.

example.es: ¿Me la puedo probar? — Sí, el probador está al fondo.
example.en: Can I try it on? — Yes, the fitting room is at the back.

points.point: conmigo, contigo; mí and ti after other prepositions (para ti, sin mí)
points.explain: Con + mí / ti become conmigo and contigo; other prepositions take mí and ti.
points.trap: *con mí, *con ti.

example.es: ¿Vienes conmigo el viernes? Te invito un café.
example.en: Are you coming with me on Friday? Coffee's on me.

points.point: neuter lo for a whole idea (no lo sé, ya lo sé)
points.explain: Lo can stand for a whole statement or fact.
points.trap: Learners leave it out: *no sé is fine, but 'I know (that)' is ya lo sé.

example.es: —¿Vas a ir a la fiesta? —Todavía no lo sé.
example.en: —Are you going to the party? —I don't know yet.

points.point: indirect object pronouns te / le / les for the receiver (te marco, le mando un mensaje)
points.explain: Te, le and les show who receives a call, a message or a favour; hablarle a alguien means to phone them in Mexico.
points.trap: Learners drop the pronoun: *mando un mensaje a mi vecina instead of le mando…

example.es: Al rato te marco y le mando la ubicación a tu hermana.
example.en: I'll call you in a bit and send your sister the location.

points.point: le for usted in service and phone phrases (¿En qué le ayudo? ¿Le comunico?)
points.explain: Formal le to usted is normal in service phrases; it doesn't mean Mexico uses le for 'him'.
points.trap: Learners copy it for third persons: *le vi ayer (say lo vi).

example.es: Buenas tardes, ¿en qué le puedo ayudar?
example.en: Good afternoon, how can I help you?

points.point: algo / nada, alguien / nadie, algún / ningún; double negatives (no hay nada, no vino nadie)
points.explain: When a negative word comes after the verb, no goes before it; alguno and ninguno drop -o before a masculine noun.
points.trap: *Hay nada; and *no hay ningunos (ninguno is almost always singular).

example.es: ¿Hay alguien en la casa? — No, no hay nadie.
example.en: Is anyone home? — No, there's nobody.

points.point: ¿cuál? and ¿qué?: ¿cuál + noun? is normal in Mexico (¿cuál colonia te gusta?)
points.explain: Cuál asks for a choice; in Mexico it goes straight before a noun as well as before ser.
points.trap: Spain-based books mark ¿cuál colonia? as wrong; it isn't in Mexico. Before ser, 'what' is usually cuál: ¿cuál es tu dirección?

example.es: ¿Cuál colonia te gusta más, la Roma o la Narvarte?
example.en: Which neighbourhood do you like better, Roma or Narvarte?

points.point: relative que (la taquería que está en la esquina)
points.explain: Que joins a description to a noun and covers 'that', 'which' and 'who'.
points.trap: English can drop 'that'; Spanish can't: *la taquería está en la esquina es buena.

example.es: La taquería que está en la esquina es la mejor.
example.en: The taco place on the corner is the best.

points.point: doubling: le / les together with the person (cantarle las mañanitas a alguien)
points.explain: Spanish usually repeats the receiver: le … a tu abuela.
points.trap: Leaving out le sounds odd in speech.

example.es: Vamos a cantarle las mañanitas a tu abuela.
example.en: We're going to sing Las Mañanitas to your grandma.

points.point: double object pronouns: le / les become se before lo / la (se lo dejo)
points.explain: Indirect comes before direct, and le / les turn into se before lo, la, los, las.
points.trap: *le lo is impossible.

example.es: ¿El paquete? Se lo dejo con el portero.
example.en: The parcel? I'll leave it with the doorman for you.

points.point: Mexican se los for 'it, to you all / to them' (se los dije)
points.explain: Mexicans often move the plural of 'them' onto lo: se los dije = I told you all (it).
points.trap: It looks like 'them' refers to the thing; it refers to the people.

example.es: Ya se los dije: la junta es a las seis.
example.en: I already told you all: the meeting's at six.

points.point: the emphatic -le in pásale, ándale, órale, córrele
points.explain: The -le adds Mexican warmth or urgency and doesn't refer to anyone.
points.trap: Don't analyse it as 'to him'; use pásale with tú and pásele with usted.

example.es: ¡Pásale, estás en tu casa!
example.en: Come in, make yourself at home!

points.point: relatives with prepositions: con el que / con la que, en el que, a quien, donde
points.explain: A preposition goes before the relative: la señora con la que hablé.
points.trap: English ends with the preposition ('the woman I spoke with'); Spanish can't.

example.es: Es la señora con la que hablé ayer; vive en la casa donde está la tiendita.
example.en: She's the woman I spoke to yesterday; she lives in the house with the corner shop.

points.point: el que / la que / los que (the one who / whoever) and quien
points.explain: El que and quien mean 'the one who' or 'whoever'; with an unknown person they take the subjunctive.
points.trap: *el quien is wrong; quien never takes an article.

example.es: El que quiera venir, que me avise.
example.en: Whoever wants to come, let me know.

points.point: impersonal uno (uno nunca sabe)
points.explain: Uno + third-person verb means 'you' or 'one' in general.
points.trap: Learners use tú for everything general, which can sound personal.

example.es: Aquí uno se acostumbra rápido.
example.en: You get used to it quickly here.

points.point: quienes, el cual / la cual and lo cual in formal speech
points.explain: Quienes means 'those who'; el cual and lo cual are formal relatives, and lo cual refers to a whole idea.
points.trap: *que after a comma referring to a whole idea: use lo cual or lo que.

example.es: Quienes vivieron el sismo del 85 todavía hablan de él, lo cual se entiende.
example.en: Those who lived through the 1985 earthquake still talk about it, which is understandable.

points.point: cuyo / cuya / cuyos / cuyas = whose, agreeing with what is owned
points.explain: Cuyo agrees with the noun after it, not with the owner.
points.trap: English 'whose' never changes; learners leave cuyo masculine.

example.es: Es un pueblo cuyas fiestas duran una semana.
example.en: It's a town whose festivals last a week.

points.point: recognising vosotros (sois, tenéis, os) and voseo (vos sos, tenés)
points.explain: Spain uses vosotros for 'you all', and Chiapas and Central America use vos for 'you'.
points.trap: Don't copy them into Mexican speech; ustedes and tú cover both.

example.es: ¿Vosotros sois de aquí? = ¿Ustedes son de aquí?
example.en: Are you (all) from here?

points.point: pronominal idioms with an empty la / las / le (regarla, arreglárselas, echarle ganas)
points.explain: In many idioms la, las or le refer to nothing in particular.
points.trap: Don't try to translate the pronoun or leave it out.

example.es: La regué: se me olvidó la junta. Pero me las arreglé.
example.en: I blew it: I forgot the meeting. But I managed.

groups.name: Present indicative (regular, stem-changing, -g- verbs; present for plans)

points.point: regular present: vivo / vives / vive (yo, tú, usted)
points.explain: The ending shows the person: -o for yo, -es / -as for tú, -e / -a for usted, él and ella.
points.trap: With usted, learners use the tú form: *¿Usted dónde vives?

example.es: Vivo en la colonia Narvarte. ¿Usted dónde vive?
example.en: I live in Narvarte. Where do you live?

points.point: me da + noun as the everyday request (present tense, not a command)
points.explain: Mexicans ask for things with ¿me da…?, a question in the present.
points.trap: English 'give me' is a command; a bare command to a vendor sounds rude.

example.es: Me da tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
example.en: Can I have three al pastor tacos, please?

points.point: costar o > ue: cuesta / cuestan
points.explain: Costar changes o to ue, and it's plural when the things are plural.
points.trap: *¿Cuánto cuesta las pilas?

example.es: ¿Cuánto cuestan las pilas? — Cuestan cuarenta pesos.
example.en: How much are the batteries? — They're forty pesos.

points.point: traer = to have on you (no traigo cambio)
points.explain: Traer means to bring or carry; no traigo means 'I haven't got it on me'.
points.trap: No tengo cambio sounds like you own no change at all; traigo is what you carry. Yo form is traigo.

example.es: Perdón, no traigo cambio. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?
example.en: Sorry, I don't have change on me. Can I pay by card?

points.point: tener: tengo / tienes / tiene (¿tiene pilas?)
points.explain: Tener is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen.
points.trap: *Yo teno.

example.es: ¿Tiene pilas doble A?
example.en: Do you have AA batteries?

points.point: nosotros and ustedes / ellos forms (nos vemos, abren, cierran)
points.explain: Nosotros ends in -amos / -emos / -imos; ustedes, ellos and ellas share one form in -an / -en.
points.trap: Spain's vosotros forms (abrís) aren't used: ustedes abren.

example.es: ¿A qué hora abren? — Abrimos a las nueve.
example.en: What time do you open? — We open at nine.

points.point: the present for plans and arrangements (¿nos vemos el sábado?)
points.explain: The present tense covers fixed plans in the near future.
points.trap: English needs 'will' or '-ing'; learners force a future tense.

example.es: ¿Nos vemos el sábado a las cinco? — ¡Sale!
example.en: Shall we meet on Saturday at five? — Sure!

points.point: ir and venir: voy / va / vamos; vengo / viene (ir = there, venir = here)
points.explain: Ir is movement away from the speaker and venir towards the speaker.
points.trap: Answering 'I'm coming!' is ¡ya voy!, because you go to where the other person is.

example.es: ¿Ya vienes? — ¡Ya voy!
example.en: Are you coming? — Coming!

points.point: tener for the features of a place (tiene dos recámaras)
points.explain: To list what a flat or place has, use tiene; hay says what exists somewhere.
points.trap: *Es dos recámaras.

example.es: El depa tiene dos recámaras y una cocina chiquita.
example.en: The flat has two bedrooms and a small kitchen.

points.point: stem changes e > ie (empiezo), o > ue (vuelvo, duermo), e > i (pido, me visto)
points.explain: In the stressed forms the stem vowel changes; the nosotros form keeps the original vowel.
points.trap: *empezo, *volvo; and the change doesn't apply to nosotros: volvemos.

example.es: Normalmente me despierto a las seis y vuelvo a las tres.
example.en: I normally wake up at six and get back at three.

points.point: -g- in the yo form: salgo, hago, pongo, tengo, vengo, traigo, digo
points.explain: A group of common verbs adds -g- in the yo form only.
points.trap: *yo salo, *yo haco.

example.es: Salgo a las ocho y hago la comida a las dos.
example.en: I go out at eight and cook lunch at two.

points.point: acostumbrar + infinitive for habits (acostumbro desayunar temprano); soler understood
points.explain: Mexicans often say acostumbro or normalmente for habits; soler is understood but more bookish.
points.trap: Learners from Spain-based books say suelo for everything.

example.es: Acostumbro comer a las tres y cenar algo ligero.
example.en: I usually have lunch at three and a light supper.

points.point: present + desde hace / hace … que for something still going on (tengo tos desde hace tres días)
points.explain: For an action that started in the past and continues, Spanish uses the present.
points.trap: English 'I've had a cough for three days' tempts *he tenido tos por tres días.

example.es: Tengo tos desde hace tres días. / Hace tres días que tengo tos.
example.en: I've had a cough for three days.

points.point: saber vs conocer: saber facts and how to; conocer people and places
points.explain: Saber is for information and skills; conocer is for being familiar with people and places.
points.trap: English 'know' covers both: 'I know Oaxaca' is conozco Oaxaca, and conocer + person needs a.

example.es: No sé manejar, y todavía no conozco el norte.
example.en: I can't drive, and I don't know the north yet.

points.point: the historical present in stories (llego a la oficina y me dicen que…)
points.explain: Switching to the present makes a story more vivid.
points.trap: Learners keep everything in the past and the punchline falls flat.

example.es: Pues nada, que llego a la oficina y me dicen que ya cerraron.
example.en: So anyway, I get to the office and they tell me they've closed.

groups.name: Ser, estar, hay (and hacer for weather)

points.point: estar for how you are (estoy bien)
points.explain: How you feel today is estar: estoy bien, está cansada.
points.trap: 'I am well' pushes learners to *soy bien.

example.es: Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?
example.en: Very well, thanks. And you?

points.point: ser for name, origin and identity (soy de…, es mi vecina)
points.explain: Who or what someone is, and where they're from, is ser.
points.trap: *Estoy de Canadá: origin is ser de.

example.es: Soy de Canadá, pero ahora vivo aquí.
example.en: I'm from Canada, but I live here now.

points.point: ser for totals and prices (son 85 pesos, es todo)
points.explain: A total is son + amount; es todo means 'that's all'.
points.trap: *Está 85 pesos.

example.es: Son ochenta y cinco pesos. — Aquí tiene.
example.en: That's 85 pesos. — Here you are.

points.point: hay for whether something exists; tener for what a person or shop has
points.explain: Ask about the place with ¿hay…? and ask the person with ¿tiene…?
points.trap: *Hay el pan dulce; and asking a vendor ¿hay…? is fine but ¿tiene…? is more personal.

example.es: ¿Hay pan dulce? — Ya no hay, pero tengo bolillos.
example.en: Is there any pan dulce? — None left, but I've got bolillos.

points.point: estar a for prices that change (¿a cómo está el kilo?)
points.explain: For daily market prices, ask ¿a cómo está…? or ¿a cómo es…?
points.trap: Fixed prices use costar or ser; estar a is for prices that move.

example.es: ¿A cómo está el kilo de jitomate?
example.en: How much is a kilo of tomatoes today?

points.point: estar for location; hay for whether one exists
points.explain: Where something is uses estar; whether there is one uses hay.
points.trap: *El metro es en la esquina.

example.es: ¿Hay una farmacia por aquí? — Sí, está a dos cuadras.
example.en: Is there a pharmacy around here? — Yes, it's two blocks away.

points.point: ser for clock time (es la una, son las dos)
points.explain: Use es for one o'clock and son for the other hours; Mexicans often ask ¿qué horas son?
points.trap: *Es las dos, *está la una.

example.es: ¿Qué horas son? — Son las cinco y media.
example.en: What time is it? — It's half past five.

points.point: hacer for weather (hace calor) and estar for states (está nublado, está lloviendo)
points.explain: Heat, cold and wind use hace; cloudy and raining use está.
points.trap: *Es calor, *está calor.

example.es: Hace mucho calor, pero está nublado.
example.en: It's very hot, but it's cloudy.

points.point: ser for what someone is like, tener for features, usar / traer for glasses and clothes
points.explain: Describe people with es (tall, nice), tiene (hair, eyes) and usa or trae (glasses, clothes).
points.trap: *Es pelo chino; and Spain's lleva gafas becomes usa lentes in Mexico.

example.es: Es alta y morena, tiene el pelo chino y usa lentes.
example.en: She's tall and dark, has curly hair and wears glasses.

points.point: estar for how food tastes (está rico); estuvo for a meal just finished
points.explain: Está rico is about this food now; ¡estuvo riquísimo! thanks the cook afterwards.
points.trap: Es rico means rich (or tasty in general), not 'this tastes good'.

example.es: ¡Estuvo riquísimo! ¿Qué lleva el mole?
example.en: That was delicious! What's in the mole?

points.point: había = there was / there were (past of hay)
points.explain: Hay becomes había for past descriptions, always singular.
points.trap: *habían muchas personas is common in casual speech but best avoided.

example.es: Aquí había un mercado; ahora hay un Oxxo.
example.en: There used to be a market here; now there's an Oxxo.

points.point: estar + adjective for feelings and states (estoy cansado, está enojada)
points.explain: Moods and temporary states take estar.
points.trap: *Soy cansado, *soy enojado.

example.es: ¿Qué te pasa? ¿Estás enojado?
example.en: What's wrong? Are you angry?

points.point: meaning changes with ser and estar (es aburrido / está aburrido, es listo / está listo)
points.explain: Some adjectives mean one thing with ser and another with estar.
points.trap: Estar bueno / buena about a person means 'hot'; say es buena persona.

example.es: La película es aburrida y yo ya estoy aburrido.
example.en: The film is boring and I'm already bored.

points.point: ser for where an event takes place (¿dónde es la posada?)
points.explain: Events take place with ser: la fiesta es en…; things are located with estar.
points.trap: *La posada está en casa de doña Lupe.

example.es: La posada es en casa de doña Lupe.
example.en: The posada is at Doña Lupe's house.

groups.name: Gustar-type verbs (encantar, doler, quedar, caer bien, faltar, parecer, antojarse)

points.point: gustar / encantar: me gusta + singular or infinitive, me gustan + plural
points.explain: The thing liked is the subject, so the verb agrees with it.
points.trap: *Me gusta los tacos; and encantar already means 'love', so *me encanta mucho is odd.

example.es: Me gusta mucho la comida de aquí y me encantan los tamales.
example.en: I really like the food here and I love tamales.

points.point: doler works like gustar (me duele la cabeza, me duelen los pies)
points.explain: What hurts is the subject and takes the article.
points.trap: *Mi cabeza duele / *me duele mi cabeza.

example.es: Me duele el estómago y me duelen los pies.
example.en: My stomach hurts and my feet hurt.

points.point: me cayó mal as a fixed past (me cayó mal la comida)
points.explain: Caer mal with food means it disagreed with you.
points.trap: Learners say *la comida me hizo enfermo.

example.es: Creo que me cayó mal la comida de ayer.
example.en: I think yesterday's food disagreed with me.

points.point: quedar for fit (me queda grande, ¿cómo me queda?)
points.explain: How clothes fit is quedar + me / te / le + adjective.
points.trap: English 'it's too big on me' tempts *es grande para mí.

example.es: Me queda grande. ¿Tiene una más chica?
example.en: It's too big for me. Do you have a smaller one?

points.point: dar + noun for feelings (me da pena, me da miedo, me da flojera, me da gusto)
points.explain: Many feelings are dar: me da miedo = it scares me.
points.trap: In Mexico me da pena usually means 'I'm embarrassed', not 'I feel sorry'.

example.es: Me da pena hablar en español, pero me da gusto practicar.
example.en: I'm shy about speaking Spanish, but I'm glad to practise.

points.point: caer bien / mal for people (me cae bien tu vecina)
points.explain: To say you like or dislike a person, use caer bien / mal.
points.trap: Me gusta about a person suggests attraction.

example.es: Tu vecina me cae muy bien.
example.en: I really like your neighbour.

points.point: faltar and hacer falta (le falta una copia; me hace falta la CURP)
points.explain: What's missing is the subject; the person who lacks it is me / te / le.
points.trap: *Usted falta una copia; and plural things need faltan.

example.es: Le faltan dos copias y el comprobante de domicilio.
example.en: You're missing two copies and the proof of address.

points.point: molestar like gustar (me molesta el ruido)
points.explain: The annoying thing is the subject of molestar.
points.trap: *Estoy molesto del ruido is understood but me molesta el ruido is the natural frame.

example.es: Me molesta mucho el ruido en la noche.
example.en: The noise at night really bothers me.

points.point: parecer for opinions (¿qué te parece…? me parece caro)
points.explain: Me parece + adjective or que gives a soft opinion.
points.trap: *Pienso que es caro is fine, but ¿qué piensas de? is less natural than ¿qué te parece?

example.es: ¿Qué te parece la nueva línea del Metrobús? — Me parece muy útil.
example.en: What do you think of the new Metrobús line? — I think it's very useful.

points.point: importar, interesar, dar igual (no me importa, me da igual)
points.explain: These also work like gustar: the thing is the subject.
points.trap: *Yo no importo is a different meaning ('I don't matter').

example.es: Depende. A mí me da igual, no me importa el precio.
example.en: It depends. It's all the same to me; I don't care about the price.

points.point: antojarse (¿se te antoja un cafecito?)
points.explain: Se me antoja = I fancy; it works like gustar with se.
points.trap: Spain's apetecer isn't used in Mexico.

example.es: ¿Se te antoja un cafecito con pan dulce?
example.en: Do you fancy a coffee and some pan dulce?

points.point: llamarse as a chunk (me llamo, se llama, te llamas)
points.explain: Names use llamarse: literally 'I call myself'.
points.trap: *Yo llamo… drops the me.

example.es: Me llamo … ¿Y usted cómo se llama?
example.en: My name is … And what's your name?

points.point: subirse / bajarse for getting on and off (me bajo aquí)
points.explain: On buses and the metro Mexicans say subirse and bajarse.
points.trap: Learners say *bajo aquí without me, which sounds like 'I go down here'.

example.es: Me bajo en la esquina, por favor.
example.en: I'm getting off at the corner, please.

points.point: sentirse as a chunk (me siento mal / bien)
points.explain: To say how you feel physically, use me siento + bien / mal.
points.trap: *Siento mal means 'I feel badly' about something.

example.es: Me siento mal, creo que tengo gripa.
example.en: I feel ill, I think I've got flu.

points.point: reflexive verbs for routines (me levanto, me baño, te acuestas)
points.explain: Actions you do to yourself take me / te / se / nos / se.
points.trap: In Mexico bañarse is to shower; ducharse sounds Spanish.

example.es: Me levanto a las siete y me baño en la mañana.
example.en: I get up at seven and shower in the morning.

points.point: reciprocal nos / se (nos vemos, se conocen)
points.explain: Nos and se also mean 'each other'.
points.trap: *Vemos el uno al otro.

example.es: Quedamos de vernos a las seis en la esquina.
example.en: We agreed to meet at six on the corner.

points.point: irse = to leave; ir = to go; regresarse and tardarse in Mexico
points.explain: Me voy means 'I'm leaving'; Mexicans also say regresarse (go back) and tardarse (take time).
points.trap: Voy alone needs a destination; 'I'm off' is ya me voy.

example.es: Ya me voy. ¿Cuánto se tarda el camión al centro?
example.en: I'm off. How long does the bus take to downtown?

points.point: reflexives for accidents to yourself (me caí, me corté el dedo, me torcí el tobillo)
points.explain: Injuries use a reflexive verb and the article with the body part.
points.trap: *Me corté mi dedo.

example.es: Me caí y me torcí el tobillo.
example.en: I fell and twisted my ankle.

points.point: verbs of change: ponerse (moods), volverse (lasting change), quedarse (result), hacerse (effort), llegar a ser
points.explain: English 'get' or 'become' has several Spanish equivalents depending on the kind of change.
points.trap: Learners use convertirse for everything.

example.es: Se puso nerviosa; él se volvió famoso y su hermano se quedó sin trabajo.
example.en: She got nervous; he became famous and his brother ended up out of work.

groups.name: Preterite (the Mexican default for any finished action, today included)

points.point: no entendí as a fixed past
points.explain: No entendí ('I didn't get it') is used as a chunk before the preterite is taught.
points.trap: No entiendo is also fine, but no entendí is what Mexicans say about something just said.

example.es: Perdón, no entendí. ¿Me lo repite?
example.en: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat it?

points.point: the preterite for anything finished, including today and this year (hoy me levanté temprano)
points.explain: In Mexico the preterite covers every finished action, today included.
points.trap: Spain-based books teach hoy he comido; in Mexico hoy comí is normal.

example.es: Hoy comí en una fonda y me fue muy bien.
example.en: Today I had lunch at a fonda and it went really well.

points.point: regular preterite yo / tú / usted: -é, -aste, -ó; -í, -iste, -ió
points.explain: Preterite endings carry the stress: llegué, llegaste, llegó.
points.trap: Stress changes the meaning: hablo (I speak) vs habló (he spoke).

example.es: ¿Ya llegaste? — Sí, ya llegué.
example.en: Are you there yet? — Yes, I've arrived.

points.point: first irregulars: fui (ir and ser), hice, estuve
points.explain: Fui means both 'I went' and 'I was'; hice and estuve have no written accent.
points.trap: *hicé, *estuví.

example.es: Ayer fui al mercado y estuve ahí toda la mañana.
example.en: Yesterday I went to the market and was there all morning.

points.point: ya and todavía no with the preterite (¿ya comiste? — todavía no)
points.explain: Mexicans ask about 'yet / already' with ya + preterite.
points.trap: English 'have you eaten yet?' tempts *¿has comido ya?

example.es: ¿Ya comiste? — Todavía no, ¿vamos?
example.en: Have you eaten yet? — Not yet, shall we go?

points.point: spelling changes in the yo form: llegué, busqué, empecé
points.explain: To keep the sound, g → gu, c → qu and z → c before -é.
points.trap: *llegé, *buscé.

example.es: Busqué mi cartera por todos lados.
example.en: I looked everywhere for my wallet.

points.point: ¿cómo te fue? / me fue bien as chunks
points.explain: Ir bien / mal with me / te / le asks and tells how something went.
points.trap: *¿Cómo fue tu día? is understood but ¿cómo te fue? is the everyday question.

example.es: ¿Cómo te fue en el doctor? — Me fue muy bien.
example.en: How did it go at the doctor's? — It went very well.

points.point: full preterite: nosotros and ustedes / ellos forms (fuimos, llegaron)
points.explain: Plural endings are -amos / -imos and -aron / -ieron.
points.trap: Regular -ar and -ir nosotros forms look like the present (llegamos); context decides.

example.es: Fuimos a un pueblo cerca de aquí y regresamos el domingo.
example.en: We went to a town near here and came back on Sunday.

points.point: irregular stems: tuve, estuve, pude, puse, hice, dije, vine, quise, supe (no written accent)
points.explain: These verbs change their stem and use the endings -e, -iste, -o, -imos, -ieron (-eron after j).
points.trap: *pudó, *dijieron.

example.es: Anoche no pude dormir y hoy vine tarde.
example.en: I couldn't sleep last night and came in late today.

points.point: verbs that change meaning in the preterite (conocí = met, supe = found out, no pude = didn't manage, no quise = refused)
points.explain: In the preterite some verbs describe a single event rather than a state.
points.trap: 'I met your neighbour' is conocí, not *encontré.

example.es: Conocí a tu vecina en la tienda.
example.en: I met your neighbour at the shop.

points.point: estuvo / fue to judge an event (estuvo muy bonito, fue increíble)
points.explain: To sum up how something was, Mexicans use estuvo or fue.
points.trap: *Era muy bonito about a one-off event sounds like a description.

example.es: La fiesta estuvo muy bonita; fue increíble.
example.en: The party was lovely; it was amazing.

points.point: y in the third person: se cayó, leyó, oyeron
points.explain: Verbs like caer, leer and oír write y between vowels in the él and ellos forms.
points.trap: *se caió.

example.es: Se me cayó el celular y se rompió la pantalla.
example.en: I dropped my phone and the screen broke.

points.point: -ir verbs change e > i and o > u in the third person (se sintió, durmió, pidió)
points.explain: Stem-changing -ir verbs change in the él / ella / usted and ellos forms only.
points.trap: *dormió, *se sentió.

example.es: ¿Cómo durmió anoche? — Mal, y en la mañana me sentí mareada.
example.en: How did you sleep last night? — Badly, and this morning I felt dizzy.

points.point: impersonal third-person plural for unknown people (me cobraron, ya me depositaron)
points.explain: Ellos with no subject means 'someone' or 'they' at the bank, shop or office.
points.trap: Learners add *ellos or reach for a passive.

example.es: Me cobraron dos veces; ya te transferí lo que te debía.
example.en: They charged me twice; I've sent you what I owed you.

points.point: the preterite in historical narrative and dates
points.explain: History is told in the preterite, with years read as numbers.
points.trap: Learners read years like English (*diecinueve diez): 1910 is mil novecientos diez.

example.es: La Revolución empezó en 1910.
example.en: The Revolution began in 1910.

points.point: the imperfect of politeness from shopkeepers (¿qué buscaba?)
points.explain: Vendors use the imperfect to sound gentle: ¿qué buscaba? = what are you looking for?
points.trap: It doesn't refer to the past.

example.es: ¡Pásele, joven! ¿Qué buscaba?
example.en: Come in! What were you looking for?

points.point: the imperfect -aba / -ía for habits and descriptions in the past
points.explain: The imperfect describes how things used to be and what you used to do.
points.trap: English 'used to' or 'would' → imperfect, not the preterite.

example.es: Antes cenaba mucho; ahora como fuerte a las tres.
example.en: I used to have a big dinner; now I have my main meal at three.

points.point: irregular imperfects: era, iba, veía
points.explain: Only ser, ir and ver are irregular in the imperfect.
points.trap: *eraba, *ía.

example.es: Antes esta colonia era muy tranquila e íbamos caminando al mercado.
example.en: This neighbourhood used to be very quiet and we'd walk to the market.

points.point: the imperfect of politeness for your own requests (quería preguntar si…)
points.explain: Quería softens a request; it doesn't mean the wish is over.
points.trap: Quiero can sound demanding to a landlord or official.

example.es: Buenas tardes, quería preguntar si todavía está disponible el depa.
example.en: Good afternoon, I wanted to ask whether the flat is still available.

points.point: imperfect for the background, preterite for events (estaba en la fila cuando se fue la luz)
points.explain: The imperfect sets the scene; the preterite moves the story forward.
points.trap: Learners put everything in one tense; the choice depends on background vs event.

example.es: Estaba en la fila cuando de repente se fue la luz.
example.en: I was in the queue when suddenly the power went off.

points.point: estaba + gerund interrupted by the preterite
points.explain: Estaba + -ando / -iendo describes an action in progress when something happened.
points.trap: Don't use it for past habits: *estaba yendo cada domingo.

example.es: Estaba esperando el camión cuando empezó a llover.
example.en: I was waiting for the bus when it started to rain.

points.point: the imperfect of excuse (¡y yo qué sabía!) and iba a + infinitive (I was going to)
points.explain: The imperfect can excuse yourself or say what you nearly did.
points.trap: Iba a decirle isn't the past of ir; it means 'I was going to tell him'.

example.es: Iba a decirle que no, pero ¡y yo qué sabía!
example.en: I was going to say no, but how was I to know!

groups.name: Present perfect (experience and change up to now) and pluperfect

points.point: the present perfect for life experience (¿has ido a Oaxaca? nunca he probado…)
points.explain: He / has / ha + participle asks and tells about experiences in your life so far.
points.trap: Not for today's finished actions in Mexico: hoy fui, not hoy he ido.

example.es: ¿Has ido a Oaxaca? — No, y nunca he probado los chapulines.
example.en: Have you been to Oaxaca? — No, and I've never tried chapulines.

points.point: irregular participles: visto, hecho, dicho, puesto, escrito, vuelto, abierto, roto
points.explain: Common verbs have irregular participles to learn by heart.
points.trap: *hacido, *escribido, *abrido.

example.es: ¿Has visto el mural de Rivera en Palacio Nacional?
example.en: Have you seen the Rivera mural in the National Palace?

points.point: Mexico: ya + preterite for 'yet', todavía no + present for 'not yet' (¿ya fuiste? todavía no conozco)
points.explain: Where English uses 'have you… yet', Mexicans say ¿ya + preterite? and todavía no + present.
points.trap: *¿Has ido ya a las pirámides? sounds Spanish.

example.es: ¿Ya fuiste a las pirámides? — Todavía no, pero quiero ir.
example.en: Have you been to the pyramids yet? — Not yet, but I want to go.

points.point: the pluperfect había + participle (cuando llegué, el camión ya se había ido)
points.explain: Había + participle puts one past event before another.
points.trap: English sometimes skips it; Spanish needs it to make the order clear.

example.es: Cuando llegué, el camión ya se había ido.
